Initial Practice Considerations for Time Limits under Proposition 45
The time limit provisions under Prop. 45 may be the most daunting components of this initiative and may raise the most perplexing uncertainties—including potential outcomes if it is not possible to complete CEQA documentation as required.
Lead agencies will be under extreme time pressure for any projects that generate substantial public interest and/or that are complex. They should understand all phases of CEQA compliance and the time involved and may need to adjust internal review time frames and review rounds for administrative draft documents.
We have addressed the need for ordinances or other mechanisms to establish “objective” thresholds and conduct completeness review. Lead agencies may also consider when project changes trigger a new review for completeness, as well as other rules that could help facilitate compliance with the time limits.
4: PRELIMINARY SCOPING PROCESS
Pursuant to Article 5, PRC Section 21024, Prop. 45 would create for qualifying essential projects an alternative scoping process to the notice of preparation and public scoping period in classic CEQA. The applicant may voluntarily choose to employ the preliminary scoping process. If the applicant does not choose this process, other scoping requirements of CEQA would continue to apply. The preliminary scoping process described in PRC Section 21024 must be completed in not more than 60 days.
An applicant would begin by providing written notice to the lead agency of its intent to complete the preliminary scoping process. The notice must present “a preliminary overview and description of the proposed essential project sufficient to inform the lead agency and the public of the anticipated features of the project.” Details like engineering plans, technical studies, or design drawings are not required. The written notice must include, to the extent known: (A) location, size, boundaries; (B) principal components and fundamental purpose; (C) general type of use, facility, infrastructure; (D) potentially affected resource areas; and (E) anticipated public agency permits or approvals. Beyond location, size, and boundaries; principal components; and type of use, facility, or infrastructure, other specifics about site plan, building height or mass, infrastructure dimensions, or other physical characteristics are not required.
After receiving the notice, the lead agency and the applicant are to hold at least two meetings to discuss the project and impacted resource areas. The lead agency will record all meetings. The lead agency must post the notice on a website so the public can submit comments by email. The applicant may, but need not, convene a public scoping meeting. The applicant must maintain a summary record of input but “shall not be required to respond to any input received.”
Benefits and Challenges of the Preliminary Scoping Provision
The benefit relates to improved efficiency of scoping with this process, in part because it focuses scoping deliberations between the applicant and the lead agency, including the need for at least two discussion meetings. Also, a maximum time frame is created for improved schedule certainty (no more than 60 days).
This process involves limitations compared with current CEQA requirements. CEQA scoping notifies and seeks important input about potential environmental effects to be studied from trustee and responsible agencies. In addition, it requires a scoping meeting for major projects (i.e., projects of statewide, regional, or areawide significance). A challenge of the preliminary scoping process is the loss of these important avenues of input about potential environmental impacts. Finally, with the allowance in this new preliminary scoping process that an applicant shall not be required to respond to scoping input, ambiguity may arise about how much the public input may ultimately influence environmental document contents. Nonetheless, applicants would be well advised to fully consider public input.
Initial Practice Considerations for Scoping under Proposition 45
Initial practice recommendations for scoping under Prop. 45 include seeking an applicant’s decision about its process choice as early as possible, determining if some other form of consultation with trustee and responsible agencies is needed, and reserving one of the applicant/lead agency meetings to consider public input and agree on environmental document contents at the end of the up-to-60-day scoping period.
5: DETERMINATION OF IMPACT SIGNIFICANCE
Currently, the determination of significance of environmental impacts under CEQA involves the use of quantitative thresholds (e.g., vehicle miles traveled, pounds per day of specified air emissions, exceedance of a certain decibel level) and qualitative thresholds (e.g., conflict with existing zoning for agricultural use, exposure to noxious odors, interfere substantially with sensitive species migratory corridors, physically divide a community, expose people to significant wildfire risks). Determination of significance is based on substantial evidence provided via technical expertise, modeling, field observations, and other sources.
Under proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(1), a public agency considering an essential project must “identify, evaluate, determine significance, and mitigate the impacts of an essential project based on compliance with existing laws.”
“Existing laws” is defined under proposed PRC Section 21028(r):
Laws in effect when the application is filed. These are “formally adopted legal requirements contained in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances” in effect on the date the application was submitted. This definition effectively freezes the standards as of that date.
An exception for later life-safety rules. A later-adopted requirement can apply only if the lead agency finds compliance is needed to address a “specific, adverse life-safety impact.” That means a “significant, quantifiable, direct, and unavoidable” impact, based on “objective, identified and written public safety standards.”
Building code updates. Updates to the California Building Standards Code, including the Fire Code, apply if they take effect before that same cutoff.
Under proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(2), an agency may have “published, adopted, or routinely used” thresholds of significance prior to the submittal of an essential project reapplication or application. This section allows the applicant to elect to vest into these thresholds. Proposed PRC Section 21022(c) also allows the applicant to waive the above requirements in writing.
Benefits and Challenges for Impact Analysis
By limiting impact determinations to compliance with existing laws, interpretations of significance are largely limited. Issues that typically require professional judgment, such as whether a scenic vista is significantly affected or groundwater overdraft is substantial, either would need to be compared to objective legal standards where they can be created or seemingly would not be evaluated for significance.
With this limitation, which is seemingly beneficial in terms of certainty in impact determinations, a number of challenges are raised. Only a limited number of agencies have formally adopted CEQA thresholds of significance that are based on existing laws as proposed under Prop. 45. Typically, agencies use PRC Section 21083(b), State CEQA Guidelines Section 15065, State CEQA Guidelines Appendix G, recommended thresholds from agencies (e.g., air districts), or recommendations of experts based on substantial evidence. In some cases, customized thresholds of significance are also created by agencies to address environmental impacts unique to the project under evaluation.
The proposed provisions under PRC Section 21022(a)(2), in combination with PRC Section 21029, may make difficult impact determinations for certain topics, including aesthetics, agricultural resources, biological resources, cultural resources, energy, land use and planning, recreation, and wildfire, that are not easily addressed through existing laws.
Although the CEQA statute and the State CEQA Guidelines would meet the definition of an existing law under PRC Section 21028(r), the use of, for example, responses to Appendix G (Initial Study checklist) to determine significance may not be appropriate when they involve qualitative thresholds (even when supported by substantial evidence), such as if a project like a large transmission line would substantially affect a scenic vista. Such a determination may involve judgment and therefore not meet the definition of existing laws under proposed PRC Section 21028(r). In addition, recommended thresholds that are not formally adopted but are based on objective standards (e.g., numeric thresholds involving air pollution provided by air districts) may also not meet the definition of an existing law under PRC Section 21028(r).
Initial Practice Considerations for Impact Significance Determination under Proposition 45
One option is that agencies could formally adopt thresholds of significance for essential projects that meet the requirements of proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(2) and PRC Section 21029. However, formal adoption may be a lengthy process and would not likely be in place in time to address essential project applications that could be submitted immediately after November 3, 2026, should Prop. 45 be approved by the voters.
6: STANDARD OF REVIEW
CEQA generally requires a lead agency to prepare an EIR whenever substantial evidence supports a fair argument that a project may have a significant effect on the environment, even if other substantial evidence supports a contrary conclusion (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15064[f][1]). The fair argument standard is one of CEQA’s defining features because it sets a comparatively low threshold for requiring an EIR.
Prop. 45 substantially narrows judicial review of CEQA challenges to essential projects. Proposed Article 6, PRC Section 21026, lays out judicial review of essential project approvals. This section applies to all essential projects and provides that “a petitioner’s claims shall be limited to a public agency’s noncompliance with objective existing laws, and the scope of the court’s review shall be limited to whether the approval or authorization complies with objective existing laws,” and “for the purpose of this subdivision, ‘objective’ means involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark or criterion available and knowable by both the applicant and the public agency before the application was submitted.” These provisions apply to EIRs and MNDs alike, raising the standards needed to overturn approval of these documents.
Benefits and Challenges of the Standard of Review Provision
The fair argument standard has long been a target of CEQA reform advocates because it sets a low bar for requiring an EIR, which is CEQA’s most comprehensive, time-consuming, and costly level of review. For the same reason, environmental advocates regard it as one of the most important tools for ensuring full analysis and disclosure before project approval. The fair argument standard has been well known for its ability to empower petitioners, whether an environmental or neighborhood group challenging an adjacent development, or a labor union or other economic interest using CEQA for leverage.
Prop. 45 eliminates the fair argument standard applied to adequacy of MNDs and places them on equal footing with EIRs. Further, by limiting review of either MNDs or EIRs to “noncompliance with objective existing laws,” litigation risk would be substantially reduced.
The challenges associated with the changes in standard of review reflect those discussed above for the “determination of significance” in that challenges may arise around both the need to adopt thresholds that conform to the initiative’s definition of existing laws and how such laws can or would be drafted to address issues typically more subjective or not based on such laws (like aesthetics, several biological resource issues, historic resources, etc.). Presumably, if no objective existing laws address these traditional CEQA issue areas, the analysis of them would not be subject to litigation challenge.
Initial Practice Considerations of the Standard of Review Provision under Proposition 45
If enacted, Prop. 45 could give lead agencies and applicants greater confidence in relying on NDs and MNDs for essential projects. Combined with the proposition’s shortened review timelines, abbreviated public comment periods, and accelerated judicial review, significant time and cost savings could result.
The same considerations for “determination of significance” surrounding the need for lead agencies to adopt standards of significance apply here.
7: ALTERNATIVES ANALYSIS
CEQA currently requires an EIR to evaluate a range of reasonable alternatives, including a mandatory no project alternative (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6). The purpose is to identify feasible alternatives that would avoid or substantially lessen significant impacts while attaining most of the project’s basic objectives. This provision gives decision-makers options and lets them compare environmental tradeoffs.
Proposed Article 5, PRC Section 21025, allows a restriction on the range of alternatives. An applicant may voluntarily elect to use the preliminary scoping process (see prior discussion of this topic, above), which includes a streamlined alternatives analysis. PRC Section 21025 permits an applicant to develop a singular alternative to the project, subject to lead agency review and comment, that is presumed to lessen impacts. The applicant’s alternative thus becomes the only alternative, aside from the “no project” alternative, the EIR can evaluate—unless the applicant proposes additional alternatives for consideration.
The alternative must take into consideration input received during preliminary scoping and be compatible with the project’s “fundamental purpose.” To the extent practicable, it must also be compatible with applicable local zoning and land use policies. The alternative need not be located on a different site (proposed PRC Section 21025[a]). It may also include different or additional components than the proposed project. Such components may consist of on- or off-site physical improvements, or alternative operational parameters or programs designed to lessen impacts (proposed PRC Section 21025[b][2][B]). Prop. 45 does not define “fundamental purpose” or explain how that concept relates to CEQA’s well-developed framework for project objectives. It also allows applicants to propose additional alternatives at their discretion (proposed PRC Section 21025[f]). However, Prop. 45 offers little guidance on how those alternatives would fit into a process otherwise built around a single applicant alternative and the no project alternative.
The lead agency must certify whether the alternative meets the requirements of Article 5 after the applicant transmits the project alternative and no project alternative. The lead agency’s discretion regarding consideration of the alternatives appears limited to certification (see above). Prop. 45 does not address circumstances where the lead agency concludes the alternative(s) do not meet the requirements of Article 5.
Benefits and Challenges of the Alternatives Provision
The benefits of the alternatives provision are less obvious than those of the initiative’s other streamlining provisions. Developing a reasonable range of alternatives takes time. Alternatives are also best formulated once the analysis has progressed far enough to identify the significant impacts they are meant to address, and it may therefore be difficult to propose feasible alternatives that reduce significant effects during a preliminary process. Prop. 45 does attempt to address some challenges with the current CEQA process. For instance, the State CEQA Guidelines require evaluation of a reasonable range of alternatives but do not define what should be considered a reasonable range. Lead agencies thus sometimes require consideration of five to ten-plus alternatives, which can add time and cost to an EIR. However, while more certainty is provided by placing limits on the number of alternatives, this provision places responsibility for developing the alternative in the hands of the party with an economic interest in project approval rather than the entity, the lead agency, that is charged with reducing the significant effects of a project via mitigation or alternatives. Under the streamlined process, both the proposed alternative and the no project alternative would largely be developed before the environmental analysis has proceeded past scoping. A project’s significant impacts may not be well understood within 15 days after scoping closes. As a result, alternatives may have to be formulated before the issues they are meant to address have been fully identified.
Prop. 45 also says little about the lead agency’s discretion once the applicant submits its alternatives. Can a lead agency require substantial revisions if the proposed alternative does not meaningfully reduce significant impacts? Can it reject the applicant’s description of the no project alternative if it believes reasonably foreseeable conditions would differ materially? Beyond noting that the lead agency must certify that the applicant has met the procedural requirements of Article 5, the initiative does not address these questions.
Initial Practice Considerations for Alternatives under Proposition 45
Lead agencies may want to develop a clear set of criteria they expect in alternatives to the project, including substantial evidence to support the criteria (such as impact reduction) so that applicants have sufficient guidance to successfully achieve the alternatives certification. Lead agencies may also consider requiring an applicant to submit a preliminary assessment of potential alternatives as part of the application process.
8: TRIBAL CONSULTATION PROCESS
In Article 3, PRC Section 21016, the initiative describes an alternative process of tribal consultation for qualifying essential projects. All essential projects must follow the alternative tribal consultation process if they use the Prop. 45 streamlining provisions, per PRC Section 21015(d)(1).
The tribal consultation process pertains to consultation with “consulting tribes,” which are defined as tribes appearing on the most recent list of Federally Recognized Indian Tribes that are traditionally and culturally affiliated with the geographic area of the proposed essential project (PRC Section 21028[e][1]). Critics, including Newsom and former Gov. Jerry Brown, have said CEQA has contributed to California’s housing shortage and high prices.
Last July, Newsom signed bills from Assemblywoman Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, and Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, to waive or streamline CEQA to build housing in already developed urban areas, and for other projects including farmworker housing, daycare centers, food banks and plants to build semiconductors, biotechnology and nanotechnology on land zoned for industrial uses.
“We needed to go bold and big on this holy grail reform,” Newsom said of the bills at the time.
Newsom has not taken a position on Proposition 45.
Wicks has endorsed it.
“We have to build for the modern era, and I think we can do so in a way that still respects our environmental values,” she said at the Capitol Weekly Housing Conference in Sacramento on Feb. 24
Wicks cited a solar company that testified in a Sacramento hearing last year that it spent 12 years, filled out 11,000 pages of environmental studies and was required to obtain 72 permits from 28 agencies to get approval for one high-voltage electric transmission line.
“We say we have these climate goals, and yet we make it almost impossible to reach them,” Wicks said. “As Democrats, we have to have an honest conversation about what we’re doing here and where our values are. And for me, as a Democrat, government has to deliver results.”
Larry Gerston, a professor emeritus of political science at San Jose State University, said the measure involves two key California concerns: Environmental stewardship and housing costs.
“Californians are very environmentally inclined,” Gerston said. “We’ve seen it again and again. They have accepted higher costs in some cases to improve air quality and support other environmental rules. Complex projects often require more extensive study, and unless technical studies are included in the application (see discussion regarding completeness review), it may be difficult to complete studies in a manner that allows the deadlines in the initiative to be attained. Simple examples include biological studies requiring species surveys tied to certain seasons, traffic studies that could rely on the inclusion of school-year data, and groundwater studies based on full-year operations. Further, controversial projects may generate hundreds or thousands of public comments needing response. In the case of an EIR, 365 business days equals roughly a year and a half. EIR practitioners are aware of the extreme challenges imposed by these time frames, especially if an applicant does not grant an extension.
Initial Practice Considerations for Time Limits under Proposition 45
The time limit provisions under Prop. 45 may be the most daunting components of this initiative and may raise the most perplexing uncertainties—including potential outcomes if it is not possible to complete CEQA documentation as required.
Lead agencies will be under extreme time pressure for any projects that generate substantial public interest and/or that are complex. They should understand all phases of CEQA compliance and the time involved and may need to adjust internal review time frames and review rounds for administrative draft documents.
We have addressed the need for ordinances or other mechanisms to establish “objective” thresholds and conduct completeness review. Lead agencies may also consider when project changes trigger a new review for completeness, as well as other rules that could help facilitate compliance with the time limits.
4: PRELIMINARY SCOPING PROCESS
Pursuant to Article 5, PRC Section 21024, Prop. 45 would create for qualifying essential projects an alternative scoping process to the notice of preparation and public scoping period in classic CEQA. The applicant may voluntarily choose to employ the preliminary scoping process. If the applicant does not choose this process, other scoping requirements of CEQA would continue to apply. The preliminary scoping process described in PRC Section 21024 must be completed in not more than 60 days.
An applicant would begin by providing written notice to the lead agency of its intent to complete the preliminary scoping process. The notice must present “a preliminary overview and description of the proposed essential project sufficient to inform the lead agency and the public of the anticipated features of the project.” Details like engineering plans, technical studies, or design drawings are not required. The written notice must include, to the extent known: (A) location, size, boundaries; (B) principal components and fundamental purpose; (C) general type of use, facility, infrastructure; (D) potentially affected resource areas; and (E) anticipated public agency permits or approvals. Beyond location, size, and boundaries; principal components; and type of use, facility, or infrastructure, other specifics about site plan, building height or mass, infrastructure dimensions, or other physical characteristics are not required.
After receiving the notice, the lead agency and the applicant are to hold at least two meetings to discuss the project and impacted resource areas. The lead agency will record all meetings. The lead agency must post the notice on a website so the public can submit comments by email. The applicant may, but need not, convene a public scoping meeting. The applicant must maintain a summary record of input but “shall not be required to respond to any input received.”
Benefits and Challenges of the Preliminary Scoping Provision
The benefit relates to improved efficiency of scoping with this process, in part because it focuses scoping deliberations between the applicant and the lead agency, including the need for at least two discussion meetings. Also, a maximum time frame is created for improved schedule certainty (no more than 60 days).
This process involves limitations compared with current CEQA requirements. CEQA scoping notifies and seeks important input about potential environmental effects to be studied from trustee and responsible agencies. In addition, it requires a scoping meeting for major projects (i.e., projects of statewide, regional, or areawide significance). A challenge of the preliminary scoping process is the loss of these important avenues of input about potential environmental impacts. Finally, with the allowance in this new preliminary scoping process that an applicant shall not be required to respond to scoping input, ambiguity may arise about how much the public input may ultimately influence environmental document contents. Nonetheless, applicants would be well advised to fully consider public input.
Initial Practice Considerations for Scoping under Proposition 45
Initial practice recommendations for scoping under Prop. 45 include seeking an applicant’s decision about its process choice as early as possible, determining if some other form of consultation with trustee and responsible agencies is needed, and reserving one of the applicant/lead agency meetings to consider public input and agree on environmental document contents at the end of the up-to-60-day scoping period.
5: DETERMINATION OF IMPACT SIGNIFICANCE
Currently, the determination of significance of environmental impacts under CEQA involves the use of quantitative thresholds (e.g., vehicle miles traveled, pounds per day of specified air emissions, exceedance of a certain decibel level) and qualitative thresholds (e.g., conflict with existing zoning for agricultural use, exposure to noxious odors, interfere substantially with sensitive species migratory corridors, physically divide a community, expose people to significant wildfire risks). Determination of significance is based on substantial evidence provided via technical expertise, modeling, field observations, and other sources.
Under proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(1), a public agency considering an essential project must “identify, evaluate, determine significance, and mitigate the impacts of an essential project based on compliance with existing laws.”
“Existing laws” is defined under proposed PRC Section 21028(r):
Laws in effect when the application is filed. These are “formally adopted legal requirements contained in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances” in effect on the date the application was submitted. This definition effectively freezes the standards as of that date.
An exception for later life-safety rules. A later-adopted requirement can apply only if the lead agency finds compliance is needed to address a “specific, adverse life-safety impact.” That means a “significant, quantifiable, direct, and unavoidable” impact, based on “objective, identified and written public safety standards.”
Building code updates. Updates to the California Building Standards Code, including the Fire Code, apply if they take effect before that same cutoff.
Under proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(2), an agency may have “published, adopted, or routinely used” thresholds of significance prior to the submittal of an essential project reapplication or application. This section allows the applicant to elect to vest into these thresholds. Proposed PRC Section 21022(c) also allows the applicant to waive the above requirements in writing.
Benefits and Challenges for Impact Analysis
By limiting impact determinations to compliance with existing laws, interpretations of significance are largely limited. Issues that typically require professional judgment, such as whether a scenic vista is significantly affected or groundwater overdraft is substantial, either would need to be compared to objective legal standards where they can be created or seemingly would not be evaluated for significance.
With this limitation, which is seemingly beneficial in terms of certainty in impact determinations, a number of challenges are raised. Only a limited number of agencies have formally adopted CEQA thresholds of significance that are based on existing laws as proposed under Prop. 45. Typically, agencies use PRC Section 21083(b), State CEQA Guidelines Section 15065, State CEQA Guidelines Appendix G, recommended thresholds from agencies (e.g., air districts), or recommendations of experts based on substantial evidence. In some cases, customized thresholds of significance are also created by agencies to address environmental impacts unique to the project under evaluation.
The proposed provisions under PRC Section 21022(a)(2), in combination with PRC Section 21029, may make difficult impact determinations for certain topics, including aesthetics, agricultural resources, biological resources, cultural resources, energy, land use and planning, recreation, and wildfire, that are not easily addressed through existing laws.
Although the CEQA statute and the State CEQA Guidelines would meet the definition of an existing law under PRC Section 21028(r), the use of, for example, responses to Appendix G (Initial Study checklist) to determine significance may not be appropriate when they involve qualitative thresholds (even when supported by substantial evidence), such as if a project like a large transmission line would substantially affect a scenic vista. Such a determination may involve judgment and therefore not meet the definition of existing laws under proposed PRC Section 21028(r). In addition, recommended thresholds that are not formally adopted but are based on objective standards (e.g., numeric thresholds involving air pollution provided by air districts) may also not meet the definition of an existing law under PRC Section 21028(r).
Initial Practice Considerations for Impact Significance Determination under Proposition 45
One option is that agencies could formally adopt thresholds of significance for essential projects that meet the requirements of proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(2) and PRC Section 21029. However, formal adoption may be a lengthy process and would not likely be in place in time to address essential project applications that could be submitted immediately after November 3, 2026, should Prop. 45 be approved by the voters.
6: STANDARD OF REVIEW
CEQA generally requires a lead agency to prepare an EIR whenever substantial evidence supports a fair argument that a project may have a significant effect on the environment, even if other substantial evidence supports a contrary conclusion (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15064[f][1]). The fair argument standard is one of CEQA’s defining features because it sets a comparatively low threshold for requiring an EIR.
Prop. 45 substantially narrows judicial review of CEQA challenges to essential projects. Proposed Article 6, PRC Section 21026, lays out judicial review of essential project approvals. Critics, including Newsom and former Gov. Jerry Brown, have said CEQA has contributed to California’s housing shortage and high prices.
Last July, Newsom signed bills from Assemblywoman Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, and Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, to waive or streamline CEQA to build housing in already developed urban areas, and for other projects including farmworker housing, daycare centers, food banks and plants to build semiconductors, biotechnology and nanotechnology on land zoned for industrial uses.
“We needed to go bold and big on this holy grail reform,” Newsom said of the bills at the time.
Newsom has not taken a position on Proposition 45.
Wicks has endorsed it.
“We have to build for the modern era, and I think we can do so in a way that still respects our environmental values,” she said at the Capitol Weekly Housing Conference in Sacramento on Feb. 24
Wicks cited a solar company that testified in a Sacramento hearing last year that it spent 12 years, filled out 11,000 pages of environmental studies and was required to obtain 72 permits from 28 agencies to get approval for one high-voltage electric transmission line.
“We say we have these climate goals, and yet we make it almost impossible to reach them,” Wicks said. “As Democrats, we have to have an honest conversation about what we’re doing here and where our values are. And for me, as a Democrat, government has to deliver results.”
Larry Gerston, a professor emeritus of political science at San Jose State University, said the measure involves two key California concerns: Environmental stewardship and housing costs.
“Californians are very environmentally inclined,” Gerston said. “We’ve seen it again and again. They have accepted higher costs in some cases to improve air quality and support other environmental rules. But it could be that people say, ‘We have to reduce costs in California, and this is one way to do it.’ I don’t know how it will go. There’s a lot at stake here.”

Complex projects often require more extensive study, and unless technical studies are included in the application (see discussion regarding completeness review), it may be difficult to complete studies in a manner that allows the deadlines in the initiative to be attained. Simple examples include biological studies requiring species surveys tied to certain seasons, traffic studies that could rely on the inclusion of school-year data, and groundwater studies based on full-year operations. Further, controversial projects may generate hundreds or thousands of public comments needing response. In the case of an EIR, 365 business days equals roughly a year and a half. EIR practitioners are aware of the extreme challenges imposed by these time frames, especially if an applicant does not grant an extension.
Initial Practice Considerations for Time Limits under Proposition 45
The time limit provisions under Prop. 45 may be the most daunting components of this initiative and may raise the most perplexing uncertainties—including potential outcomes if it is not possible to complete CEQA documentation as required.
Lead agencies will be under extreme time pressure for any projects that generate substantial public interest and/or that are complex. They should understand all phases of CEQA compliance and the time involved and may need to adjust internal review time frames and review rounds for administrative draft documents.
We have addressed the need for ordinances or other mechanisms to establish “objective” thresholds and conduct completeness review. Lead agencies may also consider when project changes trigger a new review for completeness, as well as other rules that could help facilitate compliance with the time limits.
4: PRELIMINARY SCOPING PROCESS
Pursuant to Article 5, PRC Section 21024, Prop. 45 would create for qualifying essential projects an alternative scoping process to the notice of preparation and public scoping period in classic CEQA. The applicant may voluntarily choose to employ the preliminary scoping process. If the applicant does not choose this process, other scoping requirements of CEQA would continue to apply. The preliminary scoping process described in PRC Section 21024 must be completed in not more than 60 days.
An applicant would begin by providing written notice to the lead agency of its intent to complete the preliminary scoping process. The notice must present “a preliminary overview and description of the proposed essential project sufficient to inform the lead agency and the public of the anticipated features of the project.” Details like engineering plans, technical studies, or design drawings are not required. The written notice must include, to the extent known: (A) location, size, boundaries; (B) principal components and fundamental purpose; (C) general type of use, facility, infrastructure; (D) potentially affected resource areas; and (E) anticipated public agency permits or approvals. Beyond location, size, and boundaries; principal components; and type of use, facility, or infrastructure, other specifics about site plan, building height or mass, infrastructure dimensions, or other physical characteristics are not required.
After receiving the notice, the lead agency and the applicant are to hold at least two meetings to discuss the project and impacted resource areas. The lead agency will record all meetings. The lead agency must post the notice on a website so the public can submit comments by email. The applicant may, but need not, convene a public scoping meeting. The applicant must maintain a summary record of input but “shall not be required to respond to any input received.”
Benefits and Challenges of the Preliminary Scoping Provision
The benefit relates to improved efficiency of scoping with this process, in part because it focuses scoping deliberations between the applicant and the lead agency, including the need for at least two discussion meetings. Also, a maximum time frame is created for improved schedule certainty (no more than 60 days).
This process involves limitations compared with current CEQA requirements. CEQA scoping notifies and seeks important input about potential environmental effects to be studied from trustee and responsible agencies. In addition, it requires a scoping meeting for major projects (i.e., projects of statewide, regional, or areawide significance). A challenge of the preliminary scoping process is the loss of these important avenues of input about potential environmental impacts. Finally, with the allowance in this new preliminary scoping process that an applicant shall not be required to respond to scoping input, ambiguity may arise about how much the public input may ultimately influence environmental document contents. Nonetheless, applicants would be well advised to fully consider public input.
Initial Practice Considerations for Scoping under Proposition 45
Initial practice recommendations for scoping under Prop. 45 include seeking an applicant’s decision about its process choice as early as possible, determining if some other form of consultation with trustee and responsible agencies is needed, and reserving one of the applicant/lead agency meetings to consider public input and agree on environmental document contents at the end of the up-to-60-day scoping period.
5: DETERMINATION OF IMPACT SIGNIFICANCE
Currently, the determination of significance of environmental impacts under CEQA involves the use of quantitative thresholds (e.g., vehicle miles traveled, pounds per day of specified air emissions, exceedance of a certain decibel level) and qualitative thresholds (e.g., conflict with existing zoning for agricultural use, exposure to noxious odors, interfere substantially with sensitive species migratory corridors, physically divide a community, expose people to significant wildfire risks). Determination of significance is based on substantial evidence provided via technical expertise, modeling, field observations, and other sources.
Under proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(1), a public agency considering an essential project must “identify, evaluate, determine significance, and mitigate the impacts of an essential project based on compliance with existing laws.”
“Existing laws” is defined under proposed PRC Section 21028(r):
Laws in effect when the application is filed. These are “formally adopted legal requirements contained in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances” in effect on the date the application was submitted. This definition effectively freezes the standards as of that date.
An exception for later life-safety rules. A later-adopted requirement can apply only if the lead agency finds compliance is needed to address a “specific, adverse life-safety impact.” That means a “significant, quantifiable, direct, and unavoidable” impact, based on “objective, identified and written public safety standards.”
Building code updates. Updates to the California Building Standards Code, including the Fire Code, apply if they take effect before that same cutoff.
Under proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(2), an agency may have “published, adopted, or routinely used” thresholds of significance prior to the submittal of an essential project reapplication or application. This section allows the applicant to elect to vest into these thresholds. Proposed PRC Section 21022(c) also allows the applicant to waive the above requirements in writing.
Benefits and Challenges for Impact Analysis
By limiting impact determinations to compliance with existing laws, interpretations of significance are largely limited. Issues that typically require professional judgment, such as whether a scenic vista is significantly affected or groundwater overdraft is substantial, either would need to be compared to objective legal standards where they can be created or seemingly would not be evaluated for significance.
With this limitation, which is seemingly beneficial in terms of certainty in impact determinations, a number of challenges are raised. Only a limited number of agencies have formally adopted CEQA thresholds of significance that are based on existing laws as proposed under Prop. 45. Typically, agencies use PRC Section 21083(b), State CEQA Guidelines Section 15065, State CEQA Guidelines Appendix G, recommended thresholds from agencies (e.g., air districts), or recommendations of experts based on substantial evidence. In some cases, customized thresholds of significance are also created by agencies to address environmental impacts unique to the project under evaluation.
The proposed provisions under PRC Section 21022(a)(2), in combination with PRC Section 21029, may make difficult impact determinations for certain topics, including aesthetics, agricultural resources, biological resources, cultural resources, energy, land use and planning, recreation, and wildfire, that are not easily addressed through existing laws.
Although the CEQA statute and the State CEQA Guidelines would meet the definition of an existing law under PRC Section 21028(r), the use of, for example, responses to Appendix G (Initial Study checklist) to determine significance may not be appropriate when they involve qualitative thresholds (even when supported by substantial evidence), such as if a project like a large transmission line would substantially affect a scenic vista. Such a determination may involve judgment and therefore not meet the definition of existing laws under proposed PRC Section 21028(r). In addition, recommended thresholds that are not formally adopted but are based on objective standards (e.g., numeric thresholds involving air pollution provided by air districts) may also not meet the definition of an existing law under PRC Section 21028(r).
Initial Practice Considerations for Impact Significance Determination under Proposition 45
One option is that agencies could formally adopt thresholds of significance for essential projects that meet the requirements of proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(2) and PRC Section 21029. However, formal adoption may be a lengthy process and would not likely be in place in time to address essential project applications that could be submitted immediately after November 3, 2026, should Prop. 45 be approved by the voters.
6: STANDARD OF REVIEW
CEQA generally requires a lead agency to prepare an EIR whenever substantial evidence supports a fair argument that a project may have a significant effect on the environment, even if other substantial evidence supports a contrary conclusion (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15064[f][1]). The fair argument standard is one of CEQA’s defining features because it sets a comparatively low threshold for requiring an EIR.
Prop. 45 substantially narrows judicial review of CEQA challenges to essential projects. Proposed Article 6, PRC Section 21026, lays out judicial review of essential project approvals. This section applies to all essential projects and provides that “a petitioner’s claims shall be limited to a public agency’s noncompliance with objective existing laws, and the scope of the court’s review shall be limited to whether the approval or authorization complies with objective existing laws,” and “for the purpose of this subdivision, ‘objective’ means involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark or criterion available and knowable by both the applicant and the public agency before the application was submitted.” These provisions apply to EIRs and MNDs alike, raising the standards needed to overturn approval of these documents.
Benefits and Challenges of the Standard of Review Provision
The fair argument standard has long been a target of CEQA reform advocates because it sets a low bar for requiring an EIR, which is CEQA’s most comprehensive, time-consuming, and costly level of review. For the same reason, environmental advocates regard it as one of the most important tools for ensuring full analysis and disclosure before project approval. The fair argument standard has been well known for its ability to empower petitioners, whether an environmental or neighborhood group challenging an adjacent development, or a labor union or other economic interest using CEQA for leverage.
Prop. 45 eliminates the fair argument standard applied to adequacy of MNDs and places them on equal footing with EIRs. Further, by limiting review of either MNDs or EIRs to “noncompliance with objective existing laws,” litigation risk would be substantially reduced.
The challenges associated with the changes in standard of review reflect those discussed above for the “determination of significance” in that challenges may arise around both the need to adopt thresholds that conform to the initiative’s definition of existing laws and how such laws can or would be drafted to address issues typically more subjective or not based on such laws (like aesthetics, several biological resource issues, historic resources, etc.). Presumably, if no objective existing laws address these traditional CEQA issue areas, the analysis of them would not be subject to litigation challenge.
Initial Practice Considerations of the Standard of Review Provision under Proposition 45
If enacted, Prop. 45 could give lead agencies and applicants greater confidence in relying on NDs and MNDs for essential projects. Combined with the proposition’s shortened review timelines, abbreviated public comment periods, and accelerated judicial review, significant time and cost savings could result.
The same considerations for “determination of significance” surrounding the need for lead agencies to adopt standards of significance apply here.
7: ALTERNATIVES ANALYSIS
CEQA currently requires an EIR to evaluate a range of reasonable alternatives, including a mandatory no project alternative (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6). The purpose is to identify feasible alternatives that would avoid or substantially lessen significant impacts while attaining most of the project’s basic objectives. This provision gives decision-makers options and lets them compare environmental tradeoffs.
Proposed Article 5, PRC Section 21025, allows a restriction on the range of alternatives. An applicant may voluntarily elect to use the preliminary scoping process (see prior discussion of this topic, above), which includes a streamlined alternatives analysis. PRC Section 21025 permits an applicant to develop a singular alternative to the project, subject to lead agency review and comment, that is presumed to lessen impacts. The applicant’s alternative thus becomes the only alternative, aside from the “no project” alternative, the EIR can evaluate—unless the applicant proposes additional alternatives for consideration.
The alternative must take into consideration input received during preliminary scoping and be compatible with the project’s “fundamental purpose.” To the extent practicable, it must also be compatible with applicable local zoning and land use policies. The alternative need not be located on a different site (proposed PRC Section 21025[a]). It may also include different or additional components than the proposed project. Such components may consist of on- or off-site physical improvements, or alternative operational parameters or programs designed to lessen impacts (proposed PRC Section 21025[b][2][B]). Prop. 45 does not define “fundamental purpose” or explain how that concept relates to CEQA’s well-developed framework for project objectives. It also allows applicants to propose additional alternatives at their discretion (proposed PRC Section 21025[f]). However, Prop. 45 offers little guidance on how those alternatives would fit into a process otherwise built around a single applicant alternative and the no project alternative.
The lead agency must certify whether the alternative meets the requirements of Article 5 after the applicant transmits the project alternative and no project alternative. The lead agency’s discretion regarding consideration of the alternatives appears limited to certification (see above). Prop. 45 does not address circumstances where the lead agency concludes the alternative(s) do not meet the requirements of Article 5.
Benefits and Challenges of the Alternatives Provision
The benefits of the alternatives provision are less obvious than those of the initiative’s other streamlining provisions. Developing a reasonable range of alternatives takes time. Alternatives are also best formulated once the analysis has progressed far enough to identify the significant impacts they are meant to address, and it may therefore be difficult to propose feasible alternatives that reduce significant effects during a preliminary process. Prop. 45 does attempt to address some challenges with the current CEQA process. For instance, the State CEQA Guidelines require evaluation of a reasonable range of alternatives but do not define what should be considered a reasonable range. Lead agencies thus sometimes require consideration of five to ten-plus alternatives, which can add time and cost to an EIR. However, while more certainty is provided by placing limits on the number of alternatives, this provision places responsibility for developing the alternative in the hands of the party with an economic interest in project approval rather than the entity, the lead agency, that is charged with reducing the significant effects of a project via mitigation or alternatives. Under the streamlined process, both the proposed alternative and the no project alternative would largely be developed before the environmental analysis has proceeded past scoping. A project’s significant impacts may not be well understood within 15 days after scoping closes. As a result, alternatives may have to be formulated before the issues they are meant to address have been fully identified.
Prop. 45 also says little about the lead agency’s discretion once the applicant submits its alternatives. Can a lead agency require substantial revisions if the proposed alternative does not meaningfully reduce significant impacts? Can it reject the applicant’s description of the no project alternative if it believes reasonably foreseeable conditions would differ materially? Beyond noting that the lead agency must certify that the applicant has met the procedural requirements of Article 5, the initiative does not address these questions.
Initial Practice Considerations for Alternatives under Proposition 45
Lead agencies may want to develop a clear set of criteria they expect in alternatives to the project, including substantial evidence to support the criteria (such as impact reduction) so that applicants have sufficient guidance to successfully achieve the alternatives certification. Lead agencies may also consider requiring an applicant to submit a preliminary assessment of potential alternatives as part of the application process.
8: TRIBAL CONSULTATION PROCESS
In Article 3, PRC Section 21016, the initiative describes an alternative process of tribal consultation for qualifying essential projects. All essential projects must follow the alternative tribal consultation process if they use the Prop. 45 streamlining provisions, per PRC Section 21015(d)(1).
The tribal consultation process pertains to consultation with “consulting tribes,” which are defined as tribes appearing on the most recent list of Federally Recognized Indian Tribes that are traditionally and culturally affiliated with the geographic area of the proposed essential project (PRC Section 21028[e][1]). Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. Here are our recommendations, so far, for the most competitive races and significant ballot measures on Bay Area voters’ Nov. 3 ballots. To reach our conclusions, we have interviewed more than 70 candidates for federal, state, county, city and school district offices as well as the leaders of committees supporting and opposing initiatives. Please know that, per company policy, we do not endorse in gubernatorial races; and given editorial resources, we prioritize making endorsements in open-seat, or non-incumbent, races. Bookmark this page to view additional endorsements as they are published between now and election day.
Statewide offices
Lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/10/endorsement-elect-fiona-ma-states-next-lieutenant-governor/)
Success as this state’s No. 2 requires understanding its levers of power. Currently treasurer, Fiona Ma already knows how to leverage them. The next lieutenant governor must be as capable of navigating uncharted waters as the governor whom she or he might need to replace at a moment’s notice. By that standard, Fiona Ma is eminently qualified.
(Our interviews with the two candidates for lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma and Gloria Romero — are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/25/in-their-words-fiona-ma-v-gloria-romero-we-asked-they-answered/).)
Treasurer — Eleni Kounalakis (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/endorsement-elect-eleni-kounalakis-californias-next-treasurer/)
California’s next treasurer should expect to inherit the most financially volatile environment since the Great Recession. The state faces long-running structural shortfalls. Growing federal deficits will likely drive up the state’s borrowing costs. Counties are scrambling to fill gaps in once-federally funded services. Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis’ record in business, politics and diplomacy is public and extensive. There are few blanks to fill in. The challenges awaiting the next treasurer require a tested policy and economic operator. That is Lt. Gov. Kounalakis.
(Our interview with Eleni Kounalakis is here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/in-their-words-kounalakis-caballero-tell-us-why-they-can-manage-californias-162-billion/). Jennifer Hawks would not complete our interview request or provide her resume after repeated requests.)
Insurance commissioner — Ben Allen (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/endorsement-elect-ben-allen-californias-next-insurance-commissioner/)
Bay Area voters must understand: When they choose termed-out Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara’s successor, the viability of homeownership is what’s really on the ballot. The conditions for deadlier and most destructive wildfires keep growing. And there is no end in sight. There is only one candidate who grasps the complexity of this crisis and has the legislative experience to address it. That is Ben Allen.
(Our interviews with insurance commissioner candidates Ben Allen and Jane Kim are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/in-their-words-these-candidates-want-to-control-your-home-insurance-heres-why-and-what-theyll-do/).)
Superintendent of Public Instruction — Richard Barrera (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-elect-richard-barrera-californias-superintendent-of-public-instruction-november-election-california-public-schools-sonja-shaw/)
California schools face a constellation of challenges, including declining enrollment, shrinking budgets and persistent achievement gaps. Richard Barrera is a detail-oriented incrementalist focused on student absenteeism and mental health. His opponent, Sonja Shaw, is a brash culture warrior more interested in girls’ locker rooms than the nitty gritty of school reform. We support Barrera.
(Our interviews with Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/richard-barrera-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/) and here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/sonja-shaw-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/), respectively.)
