Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Pursuant to Elections Code Section 9005, we have reviewed the proposed initiative to modify existing processes related to time limits, environmental reviews, and judicial reviews for certain types of infrastructure projects (A.G. File No. 25-0023, Amendment #1).
Background
California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Enacted in 1970, CEQA is a California law that requires state and local government agencies to consider and make public the environmental impacts of their decisions when approving or carrying out a project. Unlike other environmental laws that are focused on one issue (such as air quality), CEQA and its implementing guidelines require government agencies to consider a public or private project's total impact on the environment before approving it. CEQA applies to many types of public and private sector projects-from housing development to habitat restoration-if they have the potential to affect the environment and require "discretionary" public approval (where the agency must evaluate the project and exercise judgment).
How the CEQA Environmental Review Process Works. The CEQA process begins when a project application is submitted to a government agency for review and approval. Applicants could be private parties (such as developers) or a local or state government agency. The reviewing agency, known as the lead agency, could be part of local government (such as a city planning department) or state government (such as the California Department of Transportation). In some cases, the project applicant and the lead agency could be the same entity. For example, a city proposing upgrades to its public water system also would serve as the lead agency to identify and find ways to reduce the project's environmental impacts. At a high level, the CEQA environmental review process generally includes the following steps:
Determine if CEQA Applies. If the project requires discretionary government approval or is supported with public funds and could cause a physical change to the environment, CEQA applies, with some exceptions. For example, certain types of housing projects are statutorily exempt from the CEQA process.
Conduct Initial Study. Generally, if the project is not exempt, the lead agency conducts an initial study to determine whether the project may have a significant environmental impact and what type of environmental document is needed. For example, if the initial study finds the project would not have significant impacts on the environment, then generally no additional environmental analysis is needed. In some cases, the lead agency could require minor project modifications to reduce or avoid environmental impacts. Most projects fall into these categories. Conversely, if the project would have significant environmental impacts, some of which cannot be avoided or mitigated, the agency must develop a more detailed analysis of the environmental effects known as an environmental impact report (EIR). The EIR is the lengthiest and most time-intensive of the environmental documents to prepare, but also the least common.
Prepare Environmental Review Document and Collect Public Comment. If an environmental review document is required, the lead agency oversees it and is responsible for its findings. For example, an EIR provides detailed information to public agencies and the public about the effects the proposed project likely will have on the environment, potential ways to reduce significant effects, and possible alternatives to the project. The EIR must describe a "range of reasonable alternatives" to the project or its location. A reasonable alternative would achieve most of the project goals but reduce the environmental impact. The lead agency releases the draft EIR for public comment and must respond to all public comments before issuing a final EIR.
Approve the Environmental Review Document and Project. The lead agency decides on whether to approve the environmental document and ultimately whether to approve the project or an alternative to the project.
Other Project Permits and the Permit Streamlining Act (PSA). In addition to completing a CEQA review, applicants wishing to implement a new project typically must obtain a number of permits requiring discretionary approval from one or more government agencies. These might include, for example, a local "conditional use" permit. Enacted by the state Legislature in 1977, the PSA sets time limits for state and local government agencies-both lead agencies and responsible agencies-to make decisions about development permit applications. (A responsible agency is a state or local government agency, other than the lead agency, that has responsibility for approving or carrying out part of the project, such as by issuing a permit.) Permits cannot be issued until the CEQA process has been completed.
Legal Challenges to Agency Decisions. A lead agency's CEQA decisions can be challenged in court by project opponents. These lawsuits often argue that the agency used the wrong type of environmental document, did not properly analyze environmental impacts or project alternatives, or did not follow required procedures. If a court finds that a lead agency made a CEQA error, it can order the agency to correct the error and reconsider the project. In some cases, CEQA challenges may continue into later phases of the project, including during construction, if the agency makes later decisions that rely on earlier CEQA approvals.
Proposal
Creates New Environmental Review and Permitting Process for "Essential" Projects. As described below, this measure would modify three components of the existing CEQA- and PSA-related processes-time limits, environmental reviews, and judicial reviews-for a variety of development projects it defines as essential. The following types of projects-and their associated infrastructure-would be considered essential and eligible for the new processes: housing, water systems (not including Delta conveyance facilities), clean energy, medical treatment facilities, public safety (including first responder facilities and wildfire risk reduction, but not including jails or prisons), broadband Internet access, education facilities, and transportation (not including high-speed rail). It would require an applicant choosing to use the new processes for an essential project to comply with certain labor requirements. The measure also allows essential project applicants that had submitted their applications prior to this measure taking effect to withdraw their applications and resubmit them in order to use the new process.
Time Limits
The measure would set new time limits in state law for environmental review, permitting, and court proceedings. While certain time limits would be somewhat similar to those in current law, the measure would create options for the project applicant to challenge the agency on missed deadlines or negative decisions. The major changes proposed are described below.
Applies 30-Day Application Completeness Time Limit to More Projects. The measure would apply a 30-day time limit for lead or responsible agencies to determine whether an application for an essential project is complete, including those projects needing local general plan or zoning changes. (General plans and zoning rules-which require approval by local elected officials-guide land use planning and development at the local level.) Currently, application completeness time limits are in statute in the PSA (not in CEQA), and they do not apply to projects requiring general plan or zoning changes. Under the measure, if the agency fails to make a decision within 30 days, the application would automatically be deemed complete.
Modifies Time Limits for Environmental Review. The measure includes two main changes to how time limits for environmental review are handled. First, it extends time limits by using business days instead of calendar days. For example, it would allow lead agencies 90 business days to determine if a project is exempt from environmental review and 365 business days to determine whether to certify an EIR. Second, the measure provides the project applicant with options should the lead agency fail to meet the time limits. For example, although the applicant could consent to provide the agency additional time, the measure would also allow the applicant the option of requesting a meeting or hearing, which the agency would have to hold within 60 days. The measure would require the lead agency to approve or deny the project at the meeting or hearing. This change could have the ultimate effect of shortening the overall time for environmental reviews compared to current law. In addition, if the agency fails to meet any time limits or denies the project, the applicant could challenge these actions in court. (Currently, nothing specific happens if an agency misses statutory review time limits and they can be extended upon mutual agreement.)
Reduces the Number of Days to Make Permit Decisions. The proposed initiative would establish two different time limits for permit decisions on essential projects-one for lead agencies and one for responsible agencies.
The measure would require a lead agency to make permit decisions at the same time that it completes its environmental review, or determines the project is exempt from environmental review. This is shorter than existing time limits.
The measure would require a responsible agency to make permit decisions before one of the following, whichever happens later: either 90 days from the agency determining the permit application is complete, or within one day of the lead agency approving the overall project. This also is shorter than existing time limits.
Additionally, under the measure, if an agency misses its deadline, the applicant could consent to provide it with additional review time. Alternatively, the applicant could request a meeting or hearing, which the agency then must hold within 45 days. The agency must make a final decision at this meeting or hearing. If the agency misses any deadlines or denies the permit, the applicant could challenge these actions in court.
Sets a Time Limit for Court Proceedings Review. For essential projects, the initiative would require courts to resolve all legal challenges to project approvals, including appeals, within 270 days. The court would have the option to extend this deadline by an additional 90 days. Otherwise, the deadline could only be extended if all parties agreed to do so. Under current law, the court generally has no time limit for reaching a decision when an agency is challenged for environmental review or permitting decisions. (An exception concerns certain housing and large environmental projects that have been certified by the Governor, which currently have a 270-day time limit, to the extent feasible by the courts.)
Environmental Review
The measure would modify the environmental review process in several key ways, including:
Changes Public Comment Periods. For essential projects, the initiative would make several changes to current public comment rules. Two of the more significant changes include capping the number of days an agency must provide for public comment-such as 45 days for draft EIRs-and specifying that these periods may only be extended by a court order. By comparison, current law sets a minimum number of days for public comment (not a maximum) and allows extensions without court orders.
Offers Optional Preliminary Scoping and Single Alternative Analysis. The measure includes two notable changes related to the scope of the CEQA analysis. First, it would allow an essential project applicant to use an optional preliminary scoping process, including providing the lead agency with certain information about the project and meeting with the lead agency at least twice to discuss the project, potential alternatives, and potential environmental impacts. Second, the measure would allow the applicant, upon completing the preliminary scoping process, to develop a single project alternative. When the lead agency later prepares the EIR, it would consider this single alternative and would not be required to develop other alternatives. (Under current law, if an EIR is required, the lead agency must develop and consider a range of reasonable alternatives to the project or its location to avoid or reduce environmental impacts to less than significant levels.)
Modifies How Public Agencies Determine the Environmental Impacts of a Project. The measure requires public agencies to evaluate a project's environmental impacts-including the significance of these impacts and potential ways to reduce them-based on the project's compliance with existing laws and existing "thresholds of significance," if the agency has adopted or used such benchmarks for assessing the magnitude of various environmental impacts. This differs from existing law in that agencies currently have flexibility in selecting which thresholds to use in their environmental impacts reviews, including standards that might be developed after a project application is submitted. In addition, thresholds currently can be adopted on a project-specific basis.
Modifies Tribal Consultation Requirements. Consistent with current law, the measure requires that California native tribes be consulted about potential projects as part of the CEQA process. However, the measure makes several changes to these requirements. First, it would require applicants and lead agencies to base their tribal consultations on the list of federally recognized tribes, rather than on the longer contact list maintained by the state Native American Heritage Commission. Second, the measure would require applicants to undergo a new initial screening process with the lead agency and tribes whose cultural resources may be affected by the project. This would include identifying ways to reduce or avoid impacts to these resources. Following initial screening, formal tribal consultation-as required under current law-would take place. The measure would require that any agreed-upon measures to reduce or avoid an impact to a tribal cultural resource be included as an enforceable requirement of the project. It also would make lead agency approval of an essential project contingent on having conducted and concluded "good-faith consultation" with tribes.
Judicial Review
The proposed initiative would make several changes to the grounds on which an entity can legally challenge an agency's approval or authorization of a project and to how the courts review cases.
Changes the Court's Review of Environmental Analysis. The measure changes the legal standard that courts may use when reviewing challenges to a lead agency's decision about what type of environmental review document needs to be developed. The change effectively would give the lead agency more discretion to make this decision, and thereby make it more difficult for project opponents to successfully challenge an agency's decision. In addition, under the measure's new provisions, a petitioner's challenge to an agency's approval of an essential project could only concern an agency's noncompliance with "objective existing laws." The court's scope of review would be limited to the same, more narrow, parameters. Under current law, the court can use its independent judgment to determine whether an agency appropriately applied CEQA.
Limits the Contents of the Administrative Record. Courts use what is called an "administrative record" when reviewing CEQA cases. The measure would limit the administrative record to a specific set of information, including, for example, documents the lead agency is required to make public, public comments (and lead agency responses to them), and applicant responses to the lead agency's questions about project compliance. In contrast, under current law, CEQA requires the administrative record to include all of the information an agency used to comply with CEQA in making its decisions, which in addition to the above information might include further correspondence between the agency and applicant, internal agency communications, and written evidence submitted to the agency, among other information.
Limits the Court's Ability to Delay or Stop Projects. The measure would reduce the court's ability to delay or stop essential projects in three ways. First, if a court finds that a public agency's approval or authorization of a project was not supported by substantial evidence, it cannot rescind project approval. Instead, it could only stop the part of the project that was affected by the agency's noncompliance, and only until the error is corrected. (Currently, courts can void an agency's approval in whole or in part.) In addition, other parts of the project that were not included in the court order could not be challenged later, as they can currently. Second, if the agency's project approval was not challenged, the initiative would prevent CEQA challenges to later project actions (from implementation through construction). (Currently, CEQA challenges can be brought later in the project, sometimes even after construction has begun.) Third, the measure would allow the court to temporarily stop any part of an essential project that posed a public safety risk (until the issue was addressed), but would not allow the court to stop the project overall.

Initial Costs for State and Local Agencies. In the initial years of implementing the measure, state and local agencies likely would incur some increased administrative and legal costs. Here are our recommendations, so far, for the most competitive races and significant ballot measures on Bay Area voters’ Nov. 3 ballots. To reach our conclusions, we have interviewed more than 70 candidates for federal, state, county, city and school district offices as well as the leaders of committees supporting and opposing initiatives. Please know that, per company policy, we do not endorse in gubernatorial races; and given editorial resources, we prioritize making endorsements in open-seat, or non-incumbent, races. Bookmark this page to view additional endorsements as they are published between now and election day.
Statewide offices
Lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/10/endorsement-elect-fiona-ma-states-next-lieutenant-governor/)
Success as this state’s No. 2 requires understanding its levers of power. Currently treasurer, Fiona Ma already knows how to leverage them. The next lieutenant governor must be as capable of navigating uncharted waters as the governor whom she or he might need to replace at a moment’s notice. By that standard, Fiona Ma is eminently qualified.
(Our interviews with the two candidates for lieutenant governor — Fiona Ma and Gloria Romero — are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/25/in-their-words-fiona-ma-v-gloria-romero-we-asked-they-answered/).)
Treasurer — Eleni Kounalakis (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/endorsement-elect-eleni-kounalakis-californias-next-treasurer/)
California’s next treasurer should expect to inherit the most financially volatile environment since the Great Recession. The state faces long-running structural shortfalls. Growing federal deficits will likely drive up the state’s borrowing costs. Counties are scrambling to fill gaps in once-federally funded services. Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis’ record in business, politics and diplomacy is public and extensive. There are few blanks to fill in. The challenges awaiting the next treasurer require a tested policy and economic operator. That is Lt. Gov. Kounalakis.
(Our interview with Eleni Kounalakis is here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/21/in-their-words-kounalakis-caballero-tell-us-why-they-can-manage-californias-162-billion/). Jennifer Hawks would not complete our interview request or provide her resume after repeated requests.)
Insurance commissioner — Ben Allen (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/endorsement-elect-ben-allen-californias-next-insurance-commissioner/)
Bay Area voters must understand: When they choose termed-out Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara’s successor, the viability of homeownership is what’s really on the ballot. The conditions for deadlier and most destructive wildfires keep growing. And there is no end in sight. There is only one candidate who grasps the complexity of this crisis and has the legislative experience to address it. That is Ben Allen.
(Our interviews with insurance commissioner candidates Ben Allen and Jane Kim are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/15/in-their-words-these-candidates-want-to-control-your-home-insurance-heres-why-and-what-theyll-do/).)
Superintendent of Public Instruction — Richard Barrera (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/07/endorsement-elect-richard-barrera-californias-superintendent-of-public-instruction-november-election-california-public-schools-sonja-shaw/)
California schools face a constellation of challenges, including declining enrollment, shrinking budgets and persistent achievement gaps. Richard Barrera is a detail-oriented incrementalist focused on student absenteeism and mental health. His opponent, Sonja Shaw, is a brash culture warrior more interested in girls’ locker rooms than the nitty gritty of school reform. We support Barrera.
(Our interviews with Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/richard-barrera-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/) and here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/sonja-shaw-candidate-for-superintendent-of-public-instruction-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/), respectively.)
California ballot measures
Prop. 1 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This initiative puts state taxpayers in debt for 25 years and pumps money into a bloated system. Under the best of circumstances, it would add a tiny fraction of the new housing supply needed all while doing next to nothing to solve the real problem: the inexcusably exorbitant cost of building affordable housing.
Prop. 2 — Yes
California’s budget rules perversely count saving as spending, limiting state Legislators’ capacities to bank windfalls for leaner years. That’s fiscal malpractice written into the Constitution. Proposition 2 would exempt rainy day fund deposits from the Gann Limit, double the fund’s cap and require larger deposits when capital gains revenues surge. A state with volatile tax revenues needs a bigger cushion, not obstacles to saving.
Prop. 3 — Yes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/endorsement-proposition-3-california-ballot-measure-progressive-income-tax/)
California’s richest are doing great. Over the last four decades, while the bottom four-fifths of households have seen their real incomes decline, the top 1% have seen their real incomes grow two and half times. This upper stratum now earns in a week what the middle fifth of Californians make in a year. Proposition 3 asks the Californians truly living the California dream — the highest 2% of earners — to keep paying their fair share while also helping the state avoid painful cuts to services induced by President Trump’s and House Republicans’ deliberately punitive H.R. 1, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Prop. 4 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/19/endorsement-reject-prop-4-dont-let-politicians-raid-public-funds-for-their-campaigns/)
Taxpayer dollars must stay reserved to fix municipal roads and parks, rather than finance elections.
Prop. 5 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/20/endorsement-no-on-prop-5-a-bad-idea-that-protects-the-status-quo-and-silences-independent-minded-challengers/)
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Prop. 37 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/)
This measure looks great on the surface. But all that glitters isn’t gold. It would give builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it would artificially inflate the market by putting borrowed cash into buyers’ hands. Instead of lowering construction costs, this merely helps California home buyers take on more debt in the form of second mortgages.
Prop. 38 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/endorsement-no-on-california-proposition-38-an-8-4-billion-money-grab-immunotherapy-ucla-research-ballot-measure/)

es across partisan groups (28% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 41% independents) and age groups (30% 18 to 34; 37% 35 to 54; 50% 55 and older) and is below 50 percent across regions.
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). Net Ongoing Effect on State and Local Agencies Unclear, but Likely to Result in Savings. Over the longer term, the measure could result in both costs and savings for the state and local governments' administrative and legal activities. For example, conducting initial screening with applicants and tribes, meeting newly shortened time limits (such as for approving permit applications), and handling a possible increase in the number of projects could require additional staffing. On the other hand, the new process could result in lead agencies experiencing lower costs due to considering only one project alternative, confining tribal consultation to only federally recognized native tribes, and preparing a more limited administrative record. The measure also could reduce the ongoing number of CEQA lawsuits by, for example, increasing the discretion given to lead agency decisions, limiting the administrative record, and restricting the court's ability to rescind a project's approval. The net effects of these changes are uncertain, but likely would result in savings in the longer term.
Net Effect on State Courts Could Be Costs or Savings. This measure could impact state court workload and costs in different ways, leading to uncertain net impacts. Certain provisions of the measure could lead to decreased court workload and costs. For example, the limitations on what materials may be included in the administrative record and on what actions the courts may take would reduce the amount of court time and resources needed. Additionally, the additional decision-making discretion provided to lead agencies could potentially reduce the number of cases that ultimately are filed in court. However, other components of the measure could increase court workload and costs, such as the requirement to process cases more quickly to meet the new time limits. Depending on how these offsetting factors interact, the fiscal impacts of the measure's changes on state courts could range from net annual savings that could reach the tens of millions of dollars to net annual costs that could reach the low tens of millions of dollars. To the degree costs are incurred, some of them could be covered by court filing fees.
Potential for Additional Fiscal Effects. The measure could result in some indirect fiscal effects for state and local governments, however such impacts are subject to considerable uncertainty. For example, if the measure ultimately results in environmental reviews taking less time, the state and local governments might avoid some amount of inflationary cost increases on public infrastructure projects if construction is able to be completed more quickly. Additionally, if the measure results in more essential projects being completed overall than otherwise would be without the measure, it could lead to an increase in tax revenues, such as property tax revenue. However, if the measure's modified environmental review requirements result in some projects being approved that cause unintended negative environmental impacts, some government agencies might incur costs to mitigate or respond to those impacts.
Summary of Fiscal Effects. We estimate that this measure would have the following major direct fiscal effects:
State and local government implementation costs in the tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years. Over the long term, the annual net fiscal effects are uncertain, but state and local governments likely would experience net savings due to reduced administrative and legal workload.
Net fiscal effects on state trial courts ranging from annual savings of up to the tens of millions of dollars to annual costs of up to the low tens of millions of dollars.

Prop. 40 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-reject-california-ballot-propositions-40-41-42-billionaires-tax-ai-inequality/)
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts. However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem. We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging measure — the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Prop. 41 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-reject-california-ballot-propositions-40-41-42-billionaires-tax-ai-inequality/)
The problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago. California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs. The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Prop. 42 — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-reject-california-ballot-propositions-40-41-42-billionaires-tax-ai-inequality/)
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom’s beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era’s technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open. This measure would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Prop. 43 — Yes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/17/endorsement-back-prop-43-restore-voter-approved-restrictions-on-local-taxes-proposition-13/)
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them. Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
Prop. 44 — No (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-prop-44-politics-dont-belong-in-californias-community-health-clinics-november-3-general-election-california-health-care/)
Proposition 44 would require California’s 2,000 safety net clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient care and the services that support it, and to report publicly how their money is spent. On the surface, that sounds great. However, if passed, the measure would push the majority of clinics across California into the red — many of which have spent the last six years clawing their way back from the brink of the pandemic.
Prop. 45 —Yes (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/16/endorsement-proposition-45-november3-ballot-initiative-ceqa-reform-housing-costs/)
Proposition 45 won’t transform the state’s regulatory maze overnight. But it would make California’s planning approval process fairer, less expensive and considerably more predictable.
Bay Area transit tax
Measure RTM — No (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/)
Bay Area voters, threatened with a transportation apocalypse if they don’t approve a billion-dollar-a-year sales tax increase for public transit, should just say no. Measure RTM on the Nov. 3 ballot would add 0.5% to the cost of goods for the next 14 years in Alameda, Contra Costa, Santa Clara and San Mateo counties and 1% in San Francisco. Opposing the initiative is not a vote against public transit. It’s a demand for responsible financial management.
U.S. Congress
Congressional District 14 — Aisha Wahab (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/07/endorsement-elect-aisha-wahab-to-replace-ex-rep-eric-swalwell-in-congress/)
Among the two candidates left vying for ex-Rep. Eric Swalwell’s seat, Rep. Aisha Wahab is the best choice to represent Alameda County. The U.S. Congress is no place to send a novice. Former state Senator Wahab isn’t one. As the assistant majority leader, she was the third most powerful lawmaker in the California Senate. In that chamber, the 39-year-old Democrat had a front-row seat to the affordability debates affecting this district, which includes Hayward, Fremont, Castro Valley and Livermore. There is only one reliable, proven candidate in this race. That’s Wahab. (Wahab has represented the East Bay in Congress since September after defeating Melissa Hernandez in an August runoff to temporarily occupy Swalwell’s vacant seat. The Nov. 3 election will determine who will permanently represent the district.)
(Our interviews with candidates running to replace ex-Rep. Eric Swalwell — Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez — are here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/07/candidates-14th-district-alameda-county-swalwell-seat/).)
California Legislature
State Senate District 10 — Scott Sakakihara
The Union City councilmember is a thoughtful policy wonk who provided our editorial board with detailed answers to the district’s biggest challenges: housing costs, homelessness, struggling schools, fragmented transit systems, etc. Sakakihara — a Harvard-educated US Navy Reserve officer, Democrat and former Palantir executive — explained how he would speed housing approvals, strengthen student mental health services and demand results for taxpayers’ money. His Republican opponent, Linda Price, remains a relative unknown. Price refused multiple requests to provide her resume or answer our questionnaire. Send Sakakihara to represent this diverse, million-person district, which includes Hayward, Newark and Fremont in the north and Santa Clara, Sunnyvale and San Jose in the south.
(Our interview with Scott Sakakihara is here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/26/scott-sakakihara-state-senatorial-candidate-answers-bay-area-news-groups-primary-questionnaire/).)
San Jose City Council
District 5 — Peter Ortiz (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Over the last four years, Councilmember Peter Ortiz has evolved from an activist into a governance-focused lawmaker and forceful defender of the city’s immigrants.
District 7 — Bien Doan (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Councilmember Bien Doan, a retired firefighter first elected four years ago, is ideologically idiosyncratic. Doan identifies as pro-business but he has led fights against wage theft. He’s pro-single-family housing but has defended tenant protections for mobile home residents. He told our editorial board that in his next term he would prioritize increasing police staffing and cutting business red tape. Doan’s rival — East Side Union High School District Trustee Van Le — is not a serious candidate. This is her third time running for this seat, and her main policy platform appears to be opposing Doan.
District 9 — Genny Altwer (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/27/endorsement-san-jose-needs-a-blight-fighter-elect-genny-altwer-to-city-council/)
This district in the southwest corner of San Jose – which includes Cambrian Park, Hillsdale, Kirk Park and parts of Willow Glen – does not have the same degree of vacant storefronts, job losses, blight and homelessness as other parts of this city. But it is not immune. Whoever replaces Vice Mayor Pam Foley must be able to address this 100,000-person district’s concerns while helping solve citywide problems. We believe that candidate is Genny Altwer. Altwer, 45, represents neither the status quo nor a radical break from it. Her unconventional resume should bring new thinking to old policies.
