Δ
Public agencies are responsible for comparing the effects of a range of project alternatives, including a “no project” scenario.
Agencies judge project impacts using environmental standards they choose, covering everything from noise to air pollution, and they can revise those standards as new information emerges.
The public can then submit comments and suggest project alternatives, which the lead agency must consider. Members of the public, environmental groups and other stakeholders can sue to challenge reviews they think are illegal or incomplete.
Prop. 45 would give agencies 365 business days to decide on an environmental impact report for projects the measure defines as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation, and require courts to resolve cases within 270 calendar days.
Eligible applicants could choose the new procedures or stay with the existing ones.
What supporters and opponents say
Supporters of Prop. 45 say that the current process causes unnecessary delays and expenses, (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) including the costs of reviewing late public comments and defending against litigation.
Jennifer Barrera, chief executive of the California Chamber of Commerce, said the delays are costly.
“Time is money, and the delays that we see with regards to all of the red tape and bureaucracy … it could be anywhere from six to 10 years added on to the determination of moving a project forward,” Barrera said. “All those costs are ultimately borne by the consumers.”
Dan Dunmoyer, chief executive of the California Building Industry Association, said the proposition would decrease the cost of the average home by $75,000.
“If we want to have a society where people can live and thrive, we’ve got to find the sweet spot, and we think Prop. 45 is the sweet spot,” Dunmoyer said.
Opponents — a coalition that includes environmental groups, some labor unions and the California Democratic Party — say the measure goes far beyond basic streamlining, and gives project applicants too much power, undercutting the point of CEQA. They say Prop. 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate agencies’ ability to enforce the law.
“When you’re undoing or undermining environmental review, or saying you don’t need to do as much environmental review, you can have less community input for a project,” said Aruna Prabhala, an attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity who works on the opposition campaign.
A power shift?
Prop. 45 doesn’t just make the process go faster. It also changes (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) the rules for project applicants and the government agencies overseeing the review process, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the Legislature’s nonpartisan adviser.
Applicants could choose just one project alternative for the agency to consider rather than the multiple alternatives agencies assess today. Agencies would have to judge a project’s impacts under the standards in place when the applicant applies, rather than revising them as new information emerges, and list everything an application requires up front. If an agency misses the 365-business-day deadline, the applicant could request a hearing and potentially sue.
The public and courts would have less say. Public comments would be subject to a strict 45-day deadline, and any late comments can’t be entered into the record that a judge could review if there’s litigation.
Courts could still order agencies to fix flawed reviews, but could stop only the part of a project that failed to comply, not the whole project.
Traffic flows past construction work on eastbound Highway 50 in Sacramento on Aug. 12, 2021. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo
The same rules would apply when public agencies are developers themselves. Agencies building roads or water systems, for instance, would have the option of just analyzing one project alternative and choosing the environmental rules that apply at the time of submission. If they’re sued and a court finds they made a mistake with just one piece of their review, the overall project could still move forward.
Sean Marciniak, an attorney for Hanson Bridgett, which helped the California Chamber of Commerce write the measure, said agencies would keep the power to reject projects and the measure would not override other planning or zoning laws.
“This will protect agencies in their decisions,” he said.
Why a county group is sitting this out
Organizations that represent local governments in California, including the League of California Cities and the California State Association of Counties, have mostly stayed out of the debate.
California’s rural counties say they have a problem with building housing, and they’ve historically advocated for CEQA reform.
These counties often have small populations. They’re strapped for cash and the staff needed to handle the complicated process, said John Kennedy, a policy advocate for the Rural County Representatives of California.
So when the California Chamber of Commerce proposed a ballot initiative to speed up environmental reviews, Prop. 45 at first looked like a natural fit.
“CEQA has long been misused and manipulated by a number of interest groups seeking to extract their own interests,” Kennedy said.
But the group, which represents parts of 40 counties, is sitting this one out. Its leaders voted to stay neutral; Kennedy said he suggested the group oppose it because he thinks it goes too far.
“Prop. 45 really puts the power in the hands of the project proponents, project developers, and limits local authority to require consideration of alternatives,” he said.
He worries local agencies would lose control over the standards that decide when noise, dust or runoff is significant enough to require action.
What Prop. 45 would have changed
In Richardson Grove, had the Caltrans case come up after Prop. 45, Caltrans could have benefited from a 270-calendar-day time limit on courts to resolve the case. If a court found a flaw, it could stop only the part of the project that fell short.
The case, Marciniak said, also shows how Caltrans could have used existing standards to make the review go more smoothly and quickly. In 2014, an appeals court found Caltrans’ environmental report applied no standard for judging harm to the redwoods’ roots, and noted a state parks handbook with guidelines for protecting trees from construction damage. “There are easy tweaks any agency can make to crystallize meaningful thresholds of significance,” he said.
Opponents say the case is not typical. It’s rare for a case to take so long, said Doug Carstens, an attorney who often represents environmental groups in CEQA cases. The fixes courts required made the review better, he added.
“In this instance you’re talking about trees, but Prop. 45 could also apply to an instance where there’s people,” Carstens said. “It’s a question of going too far.”
What would it cost, and what would it save
New housing construction in the Crocker Village neighborhood in Sacramento on Feb. 10, 2022. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
The measure’s backers pitch it as an answer to California’s cost-of-living crisis.
Amelia Matier, a spokesperson for the Prop. 45 campaign, said faster, more predictable reviews would let California build housing and infrastructure at lower cost.
A study by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimates state and local governments and other public agencies would see $1.5 billion in combined savings and additional revenues.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that state and local governments and courts would face initial costs in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially more than $100 million, over the first several years, partly covered by fees.
Some costs would likely decline over time, the office said, but long-term impacts are unclear. For instance, faster building would likely lower project costs, but any harmful environmental impacts resulting from quicker reviews would cost state and local agencies more.
Carstens said the savings aren’t even guaranteed, and that the Chamber of Commerce is using the affordability debate to deregulate in favor of business.
“They say it’s about affordable housing, but that’s not anywhere visible in this measure,” Carstens said. “There’s no affordability provision or requirement for addressing the needs of people who are impoverished and underprivileged.”
If Prop. 45 passes, much would be left to the courts. The measure says it should be interpreted to give “the fullest possible weight” to approving and building essential projects. Opponents say that would tilt unclear language in favor of applicants.
Marciniak said the provision is meant for situations the authors couldn’t predict.
“There is going to be confusion, but I think importantly, a judge in California is going to look at this and understand immediately what it means,” he said.

...
Permitting also imposes indirect costs through delays.
Even when direct permitting fees are fixed and predictable, time spent waiting for approval functions as a cost of production.
The NAHB estimates that permitting delays during the development phase add about $2,500 to the cost of a typical new single-family home.
That estimate is based solely on the additional interest that accrues on development loans during average permitting delays.
The NAHB delay estimate is conservative because it isolates baseline financing expenses under average permitting conditions.
It does not capture the full range of carrying costs associated with extended or highly variable approval timelines.
For example, the national architecture firm LAI Design Group estimates that regulatory delay can reduce project value by 1 to 3 percent per month.

IN SUMMARY
Prop 45 would set deadlines on environmental reviews and lawsuits for projects like housing, roads and water systems.
It would shift power toward the people proposing those projects.
That includes public agencies building their own.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
In 2014, residents and environmental groups argued in a lawsuit that a California Department of Transportation road project planned to run through Richardson Grove State Park failed to properly evaluate how it could harm the redwood trees. It still took courts a total of 15 years to resolve all of the related legal complaints before Caltrans could move forward with building.
Environmental advocates say the litigation led to changes that better protect redwood trees. But pro-building advocates point to the case as evidence that the California Environmental Quality Act and the review process it requires need an overhaul.

https://cei.org/blog/how-permitting-is-a-hidden-tax-on-housing/
A recent study from the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) calculated the cost of government regulations for constructing a new home.
According to the NAHB, permitting-related requirements add about $38,000 to the price of an average new home ($499,500), or about 7.6 percent.
That figure reflects a combination of three distinct categories of costs identified in the NAHB study.
...
Permitting also imposes indirect costs through delays.
Even when direct permitting fees are fixed and predictable, time spent waiting for approval functions as a cost of production.
The NAHB estimates that permitting delays during the development phase add about $2,500 to the cost of a typical new single-family home.
That estimate is based solely on the additional interest that accrues on development loans during average permitting delays.
The NAHB delay estimate is conservative because it isolates baseline financing expenses under average permitting conditions.
It does not capture the full range of carrying costs associated with extended or highly variable approval timelines.
For example, the national architecture firm LAI Design Group estimates that regulatory delay can reduce project value by 1 to 3 percent per month.

Prop 45 explained: CEQA overhaul could shift who holds power over building
by
Alejandra Reyes-Velarde (https://calmatters.org/author/alejandra-reyesvelarde/)
October 9, 2026 October 8, 2026
Republish

Cars drive along Highway 101 through Richardson Grove State Park in Humboldt County on Aug. 22, 2027. Photo by Brian Baer, California State Parks
IN SUMMARY
Prop 45 would set deadlines on environmental reviews and lawsuits for projects like housing, roads and water systems.
It would shift power toward the people proposing those projects.
That includes public agencies building their own.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
In 2014, residents and environmental groups argued in a lawsuit that a California Department of Transportation road project planned to run through Richardson Grove State Park failed to properly evaluate how it could harm the redwood trees. It still took courts a total of 15 years to resolve all of the related legal complaints before Caltrans could move forward with building.
Environmental advocates say the litigation led to changes that better protect redwood trees. But pro-building advocates point to the case as evidence that the California Environmental Quality Act and the review process it requires need an overhaul.
Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/) , a November ballot initiative that aims to streamline the process, would change how fights like this one play out.
At the heart of the debate over the measure is who holds power over environmental reviews. Some legal experts say Prop. 45 would shift power away from courts and the public, giving project applicants, who include developers and public agencies building their own projects, more control at key points. For public agencies, including cities, counties and state entities, it’s complicated: an agency could lose discretion when it reviews someone else’s project and gain speed and certainty when it builds its own.
The California Chamber of Commerce, the measure’s sponsor, says the measure would cut costs by speeding up building. Critics say it goes much further than streamlining.
“This is not surgical at all,” said Ethan Elkind, a climate law expert at the Berkeley School of Law. “This would be a sea change.”
How does CEQA work?
California’s landmark environmental review law, signed in 1970, requires agencies to take into account the environmental impacts of a development and help avoid them.
Over decades, developers have raised concerns about the process, arguing litigation and bureaucracy slow down needed housing. Environmental groups say it gives communities a say in how projects get built.
In response to a housing shortage and high prices, state leaders have moved to ease CEQA’s reach over housing. Most recently, in 2025, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed laws that exempt many housing (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) projects from having to go through a lengthy environmental review process.
Prop. 45 would reach housing that doesn’t qualify for those exemptions, along with roads, water and other infrastructure projects.
Contractors with PG&E work in a trench to lay underground electric cables in Placer County on Oct. 17, 2024. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
Under the current process, public agencies are responsible for reviewing the potential environmental impacts of projects. Project applicants, usually developers, present an initial study summarizing the expected impacts. The lead public agency overseeing the review decides whether the impacts are significant enough to warrant more thorough scrutiny.

Public agencies are responsible for comparing the effects of a range of project alternatives, including a “no project” scenario.
Agencies judge project impacts using environmental standards they choose, covering everything from noise to air pollution, and they can revise those standards as new information emerges.
The public can then submit comments and suggest project alternatives, which the lead agency must consider. Members of the public, environmental groups and other stakeholders can sue to challenge reviews they think are illegal or incomplete.
Prop. 45 would give agencies 365 business days to decide on an environmental impact report for projects the measure defines as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation, and require courts to resolve cases within 270 calendar days.
Eligible applicants could choose the new procedures or stay with the existing ones.
What supporters and opponents say
Supporters of Prop. 45 say that the current process causes unnecessary delays and expenses, (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) including the costs of reviewing late public comments and defending against litigation.
Jennifer Barrera, chief executive of the California Chamber of Commerce, said the delays are costly.
“Time is money, and the delays that we see with regards to all of the red tape and bureaucracy … it could be anywhere from six to 10 years added on to the determination of moving a project forward,” Barrera said. “All those costs are ultimately borne by the consumers.”
Dan Dunmoyer, chief executive of the California Building Industry Association, said the proposition would decrease the cost of the average home by $75,000.
“If we want to have a society where people can live and thrive, we’ve got to find the sweet spot, and we think Prop. 45 is the sweet spot,” Dunmoyer said.
Opponents — a coalition that includes environmental groups, some labor unions and the California Democratic Party — say the measure goes far beyond basic streamlining, and gives project applicants too much power, undercutting the point of CEQA. They say Prop. 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate agencies’ ability to enforce the law.
“When you’re undoing or undermining environmental review, or saying you don’t need to do as much environmental review, you can have less community input for a project,” said Aruna Prabhala, an attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity who works on the opposition campaign.
A power shift?
Prop. 45 doesn’t just make the process go faster. It also changes (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) the rules for project applicants and the government agencies overseeing the review process, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the Legislature’s nonpartisan adviser.
Applicants could choose just one project alternative for the agency to consider rather than the multiple alternatives agencies assess today. Agencies would have to judge a project’s impacts under the standards in place when the applicant applies, rather than revising them as new information emerges, and list everything an application requires up front. If an agency misses the 365-business-day deadline, the applicant could request a hearing and potentially sue.
The public and courts would have less say. Public comments would be subject to a strict 45-day deadline, and any late comments can’t be entered into the record that a judge could review if there’s litigation.
Courts could still order agencies to fix flawed reviews, but could stop only the part of a project that failed to comply, not the whole project.
Traffic flows past construction work on eastbound Highway 50 in Sacramento on Aug. 12, 2021. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo
The same rules would apply when public agencies are developers themselves. Agencies building roads or water systems, for instance, would have the option of just analyzing one project alternative and choosing the environmental rules that apply at the time of submission. If they’re sued and a court finds they made a mistake with just one piece of their review, the overall project could still move forward.
Sean Marciniak, an attorney for Hanson Bridgett, which helped the California Chamber of Commerce write the measure, said agencies would keep the power to reject projects and the measure would not override other planning or zoning laws.
“This will protect agencies in their decisions,” he said.
Why a county group is sitting this out
Organizations that represent local governments in California, including the League of California Cities and the California State Association of Counties, have mostly stayed out of the debate.
California’s rural counties say they have a problem with building housing, and they’ve historically advocated for CEQA reform.
These counties often have small populations. They’re strapped for cash and the staff needed to handle the complicated process, said John Kennedy, a policy advocate for the Rural County Representatives of California.
So when the California Chamber of Commerce proposed a ballot initiative to speed up environmental reviews, Prop. 45 at first looked like a natural fit.
“CEQA has long been misused and manipulated by a number of interest groups seeking to extract their own interests,” Kennedy said.
But the group, which represents parts of 40 counties, is sitting this one out. Its leaders voted to stay neutral; Kennedy said he suggested the group oppose it because he thinks it goes too far.
“Prop. 45 really puts the power in the hands of the project proponents, project developers, and limits local authority to require consideration of alternatives,” he said.
He worries local agencies would lose control over the standards that decide when noise, dust or runoff is significant enough to require action.
What Prop. 45 would have changed
In Richardson Grove, had the Caltrans case come up after Prop. 45, Caltrans could have benefited from a 270-calendar-day time limit on courts to resolve the case. If a court found a flaw, it could stop only the part of the project that fell short.
The case, Marciniak said, also shows how Caltrans could have used existing standards to make the review go more smoothly and quickly. In 2014, an appeals court found Caltrans’ environmental report applied no standard for judging harm to the redwoods’ roots, and noted a state parks handbook with guidelines for protecting trees from construction damage. “There are easy tweaks any agency can make to crystallize meaningful thresholds of significance,” he said.
Opponents say the case is not typical. It’s rare for a case to take so long, said Doug Carstens, an attorney who often represents environmental groups in CEQA cases. The fixes courts required made the review better, he added.
“In this instance you’re talking about trees, but Prop. 45 could also apply to an instance where there’s people,” Carstens said. “It’s a question of going too far.”
What would it cost, and what would it save
New housing construction in the Crocker Village neighborhood in Sacramento on Feb. 10, 2022. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
The measure’s backers pitch it as an answer to California’s cost-of-living crisis.
Amelia Matier, a spokesperson for the Prop. 45 campaign, said faster, more predictable reviews would let California build housing and infrastructure at lower cost.
A study by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimates state and local governments and other public agencies would see $1.5 billion in combined savings and additional revenues.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that state and local governments and courts would face initial costs in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially more than $100 million, over the first several years, partly covered by fees.
Some costs would likely decline over time, the office said, but long-term impacts are unclear. For instance, faster building would likely lower project costs, but any harmful environmental impacts resulting from quicker reviews would cost state and local agencies more.
Carstens said the savings aren’t even guaranteed, and that the Chamber of Commerce is using the affordability debate to deregulate in favor of business.
“They say it’s about affordable housing, but that’s not anywhere visible in this measure,” Carstens said. “There’s no affordability provision or requirement for addressing the needs of people who are impoverished and underprivileged.”
If Prop. 45 passes, much would be left to the courts. The measure says it should be interpreted to give “the fullest possible weight” to approving and building essential projects. Opponents say that would tilt unclear language in favor of applicants.
Marciniak said the provision is meant for situations the authors couldn’t predict.
“There is going to be confusion, but I think importantly, a judge in California is going to look at this and understand immediately what it means,” he said.

## Proposition 45: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
...
### Summary
Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.”
The measure sets stricter deadlines for state and local agencies to complete both CEQA and permitting reviews.
It also establishes new deadlines for issuing permits and resolving court challenges.
Eligible applicants could choose these new procedures instead of the existing process.
The process for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reviews is changed for eligible projects.
Specifically, government agencies must specify all information that an application must contain before it is submitted, limiting their ability to request additional information or project changes later.
Environmental impacts generally would be assessed using laws and standards in place when the application was submitted, rather than allowing agencies to revise review standards based on later changes.
Applicants could develop a single project alternative rather than having the agency develop and consider multiple alternatives.
The measure also limits tribal consultation to federally recognized California tribes and places maximum time limits on comments from the public and other government agencies regarding the project.
The measure also changes the guidelines and process for CEQA lawsuits.

Proposition 45: Environmental Review
Proposition 45: Environmental Review
Proposition 45: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Building an Affordable California Act
Summary
Proposition 45 began asinitiative 25-0023 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by proponent Kurt Oneto with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 21, 2025. The initiative was cleared for signature gathering on December 26, 2025. Supporters submitted signatures in April 2026 and the Secretary of State reported that the minimum signature requirement had been met in June 2026. The measure therefore qualified for the November 2026 ballot.
Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.” The measure sets stricter deadlines for state and local agencies to complete both CEQA and permitting reviews. It also establishes new deadlines for issuing permits and resolving court challenges. Eligible applicants could choose these new procedures instead of the existing process.
The process for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reviews is changed for eligible projects. Specifically, government agencies must specify all information that an application must contain before it is submitted, limiting their ability to request additional information or project changes later. Environmental impacts generally would be assessed using laws and standards in place when the application was submitted, rather than allowing agencies to revise review standards based on later changes. Applicants could develop a single project alternative rather than having the agency develop and consider multiple alternatives. The measure also limits tribal consultation to federally recognized California tribes and places maximum time limits on comments from the public and other government agencies regarding the project.
The measure also changes the guidelines and process for CEQA lawsuits. When someone challenges a government agency’s approval of an eligible project, courts would be limited in what they could consider when determining whether the agency complied with CEQA. Courts generally could not halt the entire project if they found a CEQA violation. Instead, a court could halt only the portion of the project affected by the violation while the agency corrects the problem, allowing other parts of the project to proceed.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 45 would initially increase state and local government costs, including state court costs, by tens of millions of dollars annually and potentially more than $100 million per year. These costs would result from developing new environmental review guidelines, meeting tighter deadlines, and handling legal challenges. Some costs would be covered by fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits and could potentially reduce over time.
The measure’s longer-term fiscal effects are uncertain and could be more significant. Changes to review and court challenge rules could lead to projects being completed more quickly. In these cases, state and local governments would likely have lower project costs. If more projects are completed, there could be an increase in tax revenues. However, governments could also face higher costs if projects approved under the new procedures result in negative environmental impacts that require a government response.
What your vote means
YES: Supports creating new review procedures for certain projects defined as “essential,” including stricter deadlines for environmental reviews and permits, changes to how project alternatives and environmental impacts are considered, and limits on the timing, scope, and remedies of CEQA lawsuits.
NO: Opposes these changes and keeps the existing CEQA review and court challenge procedures for these projects, including current requirements for considering project alternatives and existing rules governing environmental review timelines and CEQA lawsuits.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that current rules around projects are too bureaucratic and expensive. They claim that Proposition 45 would reduce delays and costs associated with approving essential projects, including housing, water, clean energy, transportation, schools, hospitals, and wildfire prevention projects. They claim tighter approval timelines and a faster process for CEQA lawsuits would lower project costs, protect taxpayers, and create jobs. Supporters also maintain that projects would remain subject to California’s environmental laws, local approval, and public input.
Opponents argue that Proposition 45 would weaken environmental review and reduce public input on major development projects. They contend that placing limits on CEQA reviews, public comment periods, and court challenges could allow projects to move forward without the necessary review of possible impacts on air, water, public health, and wildlife, potentially leaving taxpayers responsible for addressing environmental damage. Opponents also argue that the measure contains no requirement that faster project approvals result in lower housing or utility costs.

Proposition 45: Environmental Review
Proposition 45: Environmental Review
Proposition 45: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Building an Affordable California Act
Summary
Proposition 45 began asinitiative 25-0023 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by proponent Kurt Oneto with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 21, 2025. The initiative was cleared for signature gathering on December 26, 2025. Supporters submitted signatures in April 2026 and the Secretary of State reported that the minimum signature requirement had been met in June 2026. The measure therefore qualified for the November 2026 ballot.
Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.” The measure sets stricter deadlines for state and local agencies to complete both CEQA and permitting reviews. It also establishes new deadlines for issuing permits and resolving court challenges. Eligible applicants could choose these new procedures instead of the existing process.
The process for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reviews is changed for eligible projects. Specifically, government agencies must specify all information that an application must contain before it is submitted, limiting their ability to request additional information or project changes later. Environmental impacts generally would be assessed using laws and standards in place when the application was submitted, rather than allowing agencies to revise review standards based on later changes. Applicants could develop a single project alternative rather than having the agency develop and consider multiple alternatives. The measure also limits tribal consultation to federally recognized California tribes and places maximum time limits on comments from the public and other government agencies regarding the project.
The measure also changes the guidelines and process for CEQA lawsuits. When someone challenges a government agency’s approval of an eligible project, courts would be limited in what they could consider when determining whether the agency complied with CEQA. Courts generally could not halt the entire project if they found a CEQA violation. Instead, a court could halt only the portion of the project affected by the violation while the agency corrects the problem, allowing other parts of the project to proceed.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 45 would initially increase state and local government costs, including state court costs, by tens of millions of dollars annually and potentially more than $100 million per year. These costs would result from developing new environmental review guidelines, meeting tighter deadlines, and handling legal challenges. Some costs would be covered by fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits and could potentially reduce over time.
The measure’s longer-term fiscal effects are uncertain and could be more significant. Changes to review and court challenge rules could lead to projects being completed more quickly. In these cases, state and local governments would likely have lower project costs. If more projects are completed, there could be an increase in tax revenues. However, governments could also face higher costs if projects approved under the new procedures result in negative environmental impacts that require a government response.
What your vote means
YES: Supports creating new review procedures for certain projects defined as “essential,” including stricter deadlines for environmental reviews and permits, changes to how project alternatives and environmental impacts are considered, and limits on the timing, scope, and remedies of CEQA lawsuits.
NO: Opposes these changes and keeps the existing CEQA review and court challenge procedures for these projects, including current requirements for considering project alternatives and existing rules governing environmental review timelines and CEQA lawsuits.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that current rules around projects are too bureaucratic and expensive. They claim that Proposition 45 would reduce delays and costs associated with approving essential projects, including housing, water, clean energy, transportation, schools, hospitals, and wildfire prevention projects. They claim tighter approval timelines and a faster process for CEQA lawsuits would lower project costs, protect taxpayers, and create jobs. Supporters also maintain that projects would remain subject to California’s environmental laws, local approval, and public input.
Opponents argue that Proposition 45 would weaken environmental review and reduce public input on major development projects. They contend that placing limits on CEQA reviews, public comment periods, and court challenges could allow projects to move forward without the necessary review of possible impacts on air, water, public health, and wildlife, potentially leaving taxpayers responsible for addressing environmental damage. Opponents also argue that the measure contains no requirement that faster project approvals result in lower housing or utility costs.

Proposition 45: Environmental Review
Proposition 45: Environmental Review
Proposition 45: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Building an Affordable California Act
Summary
Proposition 45 began asinitiative 25-0023 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by proponent Kurt Oneto with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 21, 2025. The initiative was cleared for signature gathering on December 26, 2025. Supporters submitted signatures in April 2026 and the Secretary of State reported that the minimum signature requirement had been met in June 2026. The measure therefore qualified for the November 2026 ballot.
Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.” The measure sets stricter deadlines for state and local agencies to complete both CEQA and permitting reviews. It also establishes new deadlines for issuing permits and resolving court challenges. Eligible applicants could choose these new procedures instead of the existing process.
The process for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reviews is changed for eligible projects. Specifically, government agencies must specify all information that an application must contain before it is submitted, limiting their ability to request additional information or project changes later. Environmental impacts generally would be assessed using laws and standards in place when the application was submitted, rather than allowing agencies to revise review standards based on later changes. Applicants could develop a single project alternative rather than having the agency develop and consider multiple alternatives. The measure also limits tribal consultation to federally recognized California tribes and places maximum time limits on comments from the public and other government agencies regarding the project.
The measure also changes the guidelines and process for CEQA lawsuits. When someone challenges a government agency’s approval of an eligible project, courts would be limited in what they could consider when determining whether the agency complied with CEQA. Courts generally could not halt the entire project if they found a CEQA violation. Instead, a court could halt only the portion of the project affected by the violation while the agency corrects the problem, allowing other parts of the project to proceed.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 45 would initially increase state and local government costs, including state court costs, by tens of millions of dollars annually and potentially more than $100 million per year. These costs would result from developing new environmental review guidelines, meeting tighter deadlines, and handling legal challenges. Some costs would be covered by fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits and could potentially reduce over time.
The measure’s longer-term fiscal effects are uncertain and could be more significant. Changes to review and court challenge rules could lead to projects being completed more quickly. In these cases, state and local governments would likely have lower project costs. If more projects are completed, there could be an increase in tax revenues. However, governments could also face higher costs if projects approved under the new procedures result in negative environmental impacts that require a government response.
What your vote means
YES: Supports creating new review procedures for certain projects defined as “essential,” including stricter deadlines for environmental reviews and permits, changes to how project alternatives and environmental impacts are considered, and limits on the timing, scope, and remedies of CEQA lawsuits.
NO: Opposes these changes and keeps the existing CEQA review and court challenge procedures for these projects, including current requirements for considering project alternatives and existing rules governing environmental review timelines and CEQA lawsuits.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that current rules around projects are too bureaucratic and expensive. They claim that Proposition 45 would reduce delays and costs associated with approving essential projects, including housing, water, clean energy, transportation, schools, hospitals, and wildfire prevention projects. They claim tighter approval timelines and a faster process for CEQA lawsuits would lower project costs, protect taxpayers, and create jobs. Supporters also maintain that projects would remain subject to California’s environmental laws, local approval, and public input.
Opponents argue that Proposition 45 would weaken environmental review and reduce public input on major development projects. They contend that placing limits on CEQA reviews, public comment periods, and court challenges could allow projects to move forward without the necessary review of possible impacts on air, water, public health, and wildlife, potentially leaving taxpayers responsible for addressing environmental damage. Opponents also argue that the measure contains no requirement that faster project approvals result in lower housing or utility costs.

Reasonable people land on both sides, so I'd rather lay out what's solid and what's disputed and let you decide.

**What it does**
- Creates an opt-in fast track for "essential" projects: most housing (including market-rate), water, clean energy, health facilities, wildfire-risk work, broadband, schools, and transportation, including highways.
- Sets hard deadlines: 365 business days for an environmental impact report, 180 for a negative declaration, and 270 days for courts to resolve a challenge. Applicants can sue if agencies miss them.
- Lets applicants propose one alternative instead of the multiple alternatives agencies must consider now. Comment periods are capped at 45 days for an EIR and 20 for a negative declaration.
- Limits lawsuits: 30-day filing window, deferential review, and courts can halt only the noncompliant part of a project, not rescind approval.
- Doesn't exempt projects from CEQA or repeal the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, or Endangered Species Act.

**Case for yes**
- Long reviews and lawsuits are real costs for housing, water, power and hospitals, and the measure makes the deadlines enforceable.
- Prevailing-wage and workforce rules apply to most non-housing projects.
- Supporters include hospital and water groups, affordable-housing advocates, LULAC, and NAACP California-Hawaii. The LAO's full analysis says long-run savings for agencies are likely but uncertain.

**Case for no**
- It trades environmental analysis and public input for speed. The LAO notes it could lead to projects with "unintended negative environmental impacts" being approved.
- The categories are broad (ancillary infrastructure, wildfire-risk reduction, highway projects), and the measure directs that it be read to give "the fullest possible weight" to approving them.
- It's an initiative. The Legislature can amend it only by a two-thirds vote, and only in ways that further its purposes, so mistakes would be hard to fix.
- Opposed by the state Democratic Party, the state Labor Federation, the State Building Trades, Sierra Club California, and the SF Chronicle editorial board.

- **Data centers:** Supporters cite a Legislative Counsel opinion on a related statute. Critics say the broadband and "ancillary" language could cover them. A court would likely decide.

NAHB puts the pure cost of regulatory delay under 1% of price, roughly $4,000 on an average home, though its broader regulatory estimate (fees, codes, and more) is about $132,000. content.text:
I won't give a one-word answer on this one. It turns on a values trade-off: faster approval for housing, water, power and other projects versus fuller environmental review and public challenges. Reasonable people land on both sides, so I'd rather lay out what's solid and what's disputed and let you decide.

**What it does**
- Creates an opt-in fast track for "essential" projects: most housing (including market-rate), water, clean energy, health facilities, wildfire-risk work, broadband, schools, and transportation, including highways.
- Sets hard deadlines: 365 business days for an environmental impact report, 180 for a negative declaration, and 270 days for courts to resolve a challenge. Applicants can sue if agencies miss them.
- Lets applicants propose one alternative instead of the multiple alternatives agencies must consider now. Comment periods are capped at 45 days for an EIR and 20 for a negative declaration.
- Limits lawsuits: 30-day filing window, deferential review, and courts can halt only the noncompliant part of a project, not rescind approval.
- Doesn't exempt projects from CEQA or repeal the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, or Endangered Species Act.

**Case for yes**
- Long reviews and lawsuits are real costs for housing, water, power and hospitals, and the measure makes the deadlines enforceable.
- Prevailing-wage and workforce rules apply to most non-housing projects.
- Supporters include hospital and water groups, affordable-housing advocates, LULAC, and NAACP California-Hawaii. The LAO's full analysis says long-run savings for agencies are likely but uncertain.

**Case for no**
- It trades environmental analysis and public input for speed. The LAO notes it could lead to projects with "unintended negative environmental impacts" being approved.
- The categories are broad (ancillary infrastructure, wildfire-risk reduction, highway projects), and the measure directs that it be read to give "the fullest possible weight" to approving them.
- It's an initiative. The Legislature can amend it only by a two-thirds vote, and only in ways that further its purposes, so mistakes would be hard to fix.
- Opposed by the state Democratic Party, the state Labor Federation, the State Building Trades, Sierra Club California, and the SF Chronicle editorial board.

**Disputed points**
- **Data centers:** Supporters cite a Legislative Counsel opinion on a related statute. Critics say the broadband and "ancillary" language could cover them. A court would likely decide.
- **Housing costs:** The sponsor says permitting delays add $75,000 per home. NAHB puts the pure cost of regulatory delay under 1% of price, roughly $4,000 on an average home, though its broader regulatory estimate (fees, codes, and more) is about $132,000. Nothing in the text requires savings to reach renters or buyers.
- **Litigation:** A pro-reform Holland & Knight study counts about 48,000 housing units in CEQA suits in 2020. Other studies find only a few percent of projects are sued.

**Where things stand**
- PPIC's latest poll (Oct. 16–22) had it at 46% yes and 50% no, down from 49–46 yes in September. A July poll showed 73% yes, but that question didn't use the ballot wording.
- The Mercury News endorsed yes, and the SF Chronicle endorsed no. As of the latest reporting I found, Newsom and Becerra hadn't taken a position.

**How to decide**
Vote yes if your main concern is that review delays are blocking essential projects, and you trust the new deadlines and narrower court review to avoid serious environmental harm. Vote no if you'd rather keep full review and public challenges for these projects, or you think the broad definitions reach well beyond housing. The core question is which risk you think is worse: a needed project stalled for years, or a harmful one approved before its impacts were studied.

(Jane Tyska/Bay Area News Group) Jane Tyska — Bay Area News Group
Critics, including Newsom and former Gov. Jerry Brown, have said CEQA has contributed to California’s housing shortage and high prices.
Last July, Newsom signed bills from Assemblywoman Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, and Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, to waive or streamline CEQA to build housing in already developed urban areas, and for other projects including farmworker housing, daycare centers, food banks and plants to build semiconductors, biotechnology and nanotechnology on land zoned for industrial uses.
“We needed to go bold and big on this holy grail reform,” Newsom said of the bills at the time.
Newsom has not taken a position on Proposition 45.
Wicks has endorsed it.
“We have to build for the modern era, and I think we can do so in a way that still respects our environmental values,” she said at the Capitol Weekly Housing Conference in Sacramento on Feb. 24
Wicks cited a solar company that testified in a Sacramento hearing last year that it spent 12 years, filled out 11,000 pages of environmental studies and was required to obtain 72 permits from 28 agencies to get approval for one high-voltage electric transmission line.
“We say we have these climate goals, and yet we make it almost impossible to reach them,” Wicks said. “As Democrats, we have to have an honest conversation about what we’re doing here and where our values are. And for me, as a Democrat, government has to deliver results.”
Larry Gerston, a professor emeritus of political science at San Jose State University, said the measure involves two key California concerns: Environmental stewardship and housing costs.
“Californians are very environmentally inclined,” Gerston said. “We’ve seen it again and again. They have accepted higher costs in some cases to improve air quality and support other environmental rules. But it could be that people say, ‘We have to reduce costs in California, and this is one way to do it.’ I don’t know how it will go. There’s a lot at stake here.”

ence is not addressed in the initiative, although it is conceivable that a lead agency could consider the application “incomplete” if there are meaningful project changes, restarting the clock (Prop. 45 is silent on this). Complex projects often require more extensive study, and unless technical studies are included in the application (see discussion regarding completeness review), it may be difficult to complete studies in a manner that allows the deadlines in the initiative to be attained. Simple examples include biological studies requiring species surveys tied to certain seasons, traffic studies that could rely on the inclusion of school-year data, and groundwater studies based on full-year operations. Further, controversial projects may generate hundreds or thousands of public comments needing response. In the case of an EIR, 365 business days equals roughly a year and a half. EIR practitioners are aware of the extreme challenges imposed by these time frames, especially if an applicant does not grant an extension.
Initial Practice Considerations for Time Limits under Proposition 45
The time limit provisions under Prop. 45 may be the most daunting components of this initiative and may raise the most perplexing uncertainties—including potential outcomes if it is not possible to complete CEQA documentation as required.
Lead agencies will be under extreme time pressure for any projects that generate substantial public interest and/or that are complex. They should understand all phases of CEQA compliance and the time involved and may need to adjust internal review time frames and review rounds for administrative draft documents.
We have addressed the need for ordinances or other mechanisms to establish “objective” thresholds and conduct completeness review. Lead agencies may also consider when project changes trigger a new review for completeness, as well as other rules that could help facilitate compliance with the time limits.
4: PRELIMINARY SCOPING PROCESS
Pursuant to Article 5, PRC Section 21024, Prop. 45 would create for qualifying essential projects an alternative scoping process to the notice of preparation and public scoping period in classic CEQA. The applicant may voluntarily choose to employ the preliminary scoping process. If the applicant does not choose this process, other scoping requirements of CEQA would continue to apply. The preliminary scoping process described in PRC Section 21024 must be completed in not more than 60 days.
An applicant would begin by providing written notice to the lead agency of its intent to complete the preliminary scoping process. The notice must present “a preliminary overview and description of the proposed essential project sufficient to inform the lead agency and the public of the anticipated features of the project.” Details like engineering plans, technical studies, or design drawings are not required. The written notice must include, to the extent known: (A) location, size, boundaries; (B) principal components and fundamental purpose; (C) general type of use, facility, infrastructure; (D) potentially affected resource areas; and (E) anticipated public agency permits or approvals. Beyond location, size, and boundaries; principal components; and type of use, facility, or infrastructure, other specifics about site plan, building height or mass, infrastructure dimensions, or other physical characteristics are not required.
After receiving the notice, the lead agency and the applicant are to hold at least two meetings to discuss the project and impacted resource areas. The lead agency will record all meetings. The lead agency must post the notice on a website so the public can submit comments by email. The applicant may, but need not, convene a public scoping meeting. The applicant must maintain a summary record of input but “shall not be required to respond to any input received.”
Benefits and Challenges of the Preliminary Scoping Provision
The benefit relates to improved efficiency of scoping with this process, in part because it focuses scoping deliberations between the applicant and the lead agency, including the need for at least two discussion meetings. Also, a maximum time frame is created for improved schedule certainty (no more than 60 days).
This process involves limitations compared with current CEQA requirements. CEQA scoping notifies and seeks important input about potential environmental effects to be studied from trustee and responsible agencies. In addition, it requires a scoping meeting for major projects (i.e., projects of statewide, regional, or areawide significance). A challenge of the preliminary scoping process is the loss of these important avenues of input about potential environmental impacts. Finally, with the allowance in this new preliminary scoping process that an applicant shall not be required to respond to scoping input, ambiguity may arise about how much the public input may ultimately influence environmental document contents. Nonetheless, applicants would be well advised to fully consider public input.
Initial Practice Considerations for Scoping under Proposition 45
Initial practice recommendations for scoping under Prop. 45 include seeking an applicant’s decision about its process choice as early as possible, determining if some other form of consultation with trustee and responsible agencies is needed, and reserving one of the applicant/lead agency meetings to consider public input and agree on environmental document contents at the end of the up-to-60-day scoping period.
5: DETERMINATION OF IMPACT SIGNIFICANCE
Currently, the determination of significance of environmental impacts under CEQA involves the use of quantitative thresholds (e.g., vehicle miles traveled, pounds per day of specified air emissions, exceedance of a certain decibel level) and qualitative thresholds (e.g., conflict with existing zoning for agricultural use, exposure to noxious odors, interfere substantially with sensitive species migratory corridors, physically divide a community, expose people to significant wildfire risks). Determination of significance is based on substantial evidence provided via technical expertise, modeling, field observations, and other sources.
Under proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(1), a public agency considering an essential project must “identify, evaluate, determine significance, and mitigate the impacts of an essential project based on compliance with existing laws.”
“Existing laws” is defined under proposed PRC Section 21028(r):
Laws in effect when the application is filed. These are “formally adopted legal requirements contained in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances” in effect on the date the application was submitted. This definition effectively freezes the standards as of that date.
An exception for later life-safety rules. A later-adopted requirement can apply only if the lead agency finds compliance is needed to address a “specific, adverse life-safety impact.” That means a “significant, quantifiable, direct, and unavoidable” impact, based on “objective, identified and written public safety standards.”
Building code updates. Updates to the California Building Standards Code, including the Fire Code, apply if they take effect before that same cutoff.
Under proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(2), an agency may have “published, adopted, or routinely used” thresholds of significance prior to the submittal of an essential project reapplication or application. This section allows the applicant to elect to vest into these thresholds. Proposed PRC Section 21022(c) also allows the applicant to waive the above requirements in writing.
Benefits and Challenges for Impact Analysis
By limiting impact determinations to compliance with existing laws, interpretations of significance are largely limited. Issues that typically require professional judgment, such as whether a scenic vista is significantly affected or groundwater overdraft is substantial, either would need to be compared to objective legal standards where they can be created or seemingly would not be evaluated for significance.
With this limitation, which is seemingly beneficial in terms of certainty in impact determinations, a number of challenges are raised. Only a limited number of agencies have formally adopted CEQA thresholds of significance that are based on existing laws as proposed under Prop. 45. Typically, agencies use PRC Section 21083(b), State CEQA Guidelines Section 15065, State CEQA Guidelines Appendix G, recommended thresholds from agencies (e.g., air districts), or recommendations of experts based on substantial evidence. In some cases, customized thresholds of significance are also created by agencies to address environmental impacts unique to the project under evaluation.
The proposed provisions under PRC Section 21022(a)(2), in combination with PRC Section 21029, may make difficult impact determinations for certain topics, including aesthetics, agricultural resources, biological resources, cultural resources, energy, land use and planning, recreation, and wildfire, that are not easily addressed through existing laws.
Although the CEQA statute and the State CEQA Guidelines would meet the definition of an existing law under PRC Section 21028(r), the use of, for example, responses to Appendix G (Initial Study checklist) to determine significance may not be appropriate when they involve qualitative thresholds (even when supported by substantial evidence), such as if a project like a large transmission line would substantially affect a scenic vista. Such a determination may involve judgment and therefore not meet the definition of existing laws under proposed PRC Section 21028(r). In addition, recommended thresholds that are not formally adopted but are based on objective standards (e.g., numeric thresholds involving air pollution provided by air districts) may also not meet the definition of an existing law under PRC Section 21028(r).
Initial Practice Considerations for Impact Significance Determination under Proposition 45
One option is that agencies could formally adopt thresholds of significance for essential projects that meet the requirements of proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(2) and PRC Section 21029. However, formal adoption may be a lengthy process and would not likely be in place in time to address essential project applications that could be submitted immediately after November 3, 2026, should Prop. 45 be approved by the voters.
6: STANDARD OF REVIEW
CEQA generally requires a lead agency to prepare an EIR whenever substantial evidence supports a fair argument that a project may have a significant effect on the environment, even if other substantial evidence supports a contrary conclusion (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15064[f][1]). The fair argument standard is one of CEQA’s defining features because it sets a comparatively low threshold for requiring an EIR.
Prop. 45 substantially narrows judicial review of CEQA challenges to essential projects. Proposed Article 6, PRC Section 21026, lays out judicial review of essential project approvals. This section applies to all essential projects and provides that “a petitioner’s claims shall be limited to a public agency’s noncompliance with objective existing laws, and the scope of the court’s review shall be limited to whether the approval or authorization complies with objective existing laws,” and “for the purpose of this subdivision, ‘objective’ means involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark or criterion available and knowable by both the applicant and the public agency before the application was submitted.” These provisions apply to EIRs and MNDs alike, raising the standards needed to overturn approval of these documents.
Benefits and Challenges of the Standard of Review Provision
The fair argument standard has long been a target of CEQA reform advocates because it sets a low bar for requiring an EIR, which is CEQA’s most comprehensive, time-consuming, and costly level of review. For the same reason, environmental advocates regard it as one of the most important tools for ensuring full analysis and disclosure before project approval. The fair argument standard has been well known for its ability to empower petitioners, whether an environmental or neighborhood group challenging an adjacent development, or a labor union or other economic interest using CEQA for leverage.
Prop. 45 eliminates the fair argument standard applied to adequacy of MNDs and places them on equal footing with EIRs. Further, by limiting review of either MNDs or EIRs to “noncompliance with objective existing laws,” litigation risk would be substantially reduced.
The challenges associated with the changes in standard of review reflect those discussed above for the “determination of significance” in that challenges may arise around both the need to adopt thresholds that conform to the initiative’s definition of existing laws and how such laws can or would be drafted to address issues typically more subjective or not based on such laws (like aesthetics, several biological resource issues, historic resources, etc.). Presumably, if no objective existing laws address these traditional CEQA issue areas, the analysis of them would not be subject to litigation challenge.
Initial Practice Considerations of the Standard of Review Provision under Proposition 45
If enacted, Prop. 45 could give lead agencies and applicants greater confidence in relying on NDs and MNDs for essential projects. Combined with the proposition’s shortened review timelines, abbreviated public comment periods, and accelerated judicial review, significant time and cost savings could result.
The same considerations for “determination of significance” surrounding the need for lead agencies to adopt standards of significance apply here.
7: ALTERNATIVES ANALYSIS
CEQA currently requires an EIR to evaluate a range of reasonable alternatives, including a mandatory no project alternative (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6). The purpose is to identify feasible alternatives that would avoid or substantially lessen significant impacts while attaining most of the project’s basic objectives. This provision gives decision-makers options and lets them compare environmental tradeoffs.
Proposed Article 5, PRC Section 21025, allows a restriction on the range of alternatives. An applicant may voluntarily elect to use the preliminary scoping process (see prior discussion of this topic, above), which includes a streamlined alternatives analysis. PRC Section 21025 permits an applicant to develop a singular alternative to the project, subject to lead agency review and comment, that is presumed to lessen impacts. The applicant’s alternative thus becomes the only alternative, aside from the “no project” alternative, the EIR can evaluate—unless the applicant proposes additional alternatives for consideration.
The alternative must take into consideration input received during preliminary scoping and be compatible with the project’s “fundamental purpose.” To the extent practicable, it must also be compatible with applicable local zoning and land use policies. The alternative need not be located on a different site (proposed PRC Section 21025[a]). It may also include different or additional components than the proposed project. Such components may consist of on- or off-site physical improvements, or alternative operational parameters or programs designed to lessen impacts (proposed PRC Section 21025[b][2][B]). Prop. 45 does not define “fundamental purpose” or explain how that concept relates to CEQA’s well-developed framework for project objectives. It also allows applicants to propose additional alternatives at their discretion (proposed PRC Section 21025[f]). However, Prop. 45 offers little guidance on how those alternatives would fit into a process otherwise built around a single applicant alternative and the no project alternative.
The lead agency must certify whether the alternative meets the requirements of Article 5 after the applicant transmits the project alternative and no project alternative. The lead agency’s discretion regarding consideration of the alternatives appears limited to certification (see above). Prop. 45 does not address circumstances where the lead agency concludes the alternative(s) do not meet the requirements of Article 5.
Benefits and Challenges of the Alternatives Provision
The benefits of the alternatives provision are less obvious than those of the initiative’s other streamlining provisions. Developing a reasonable range of alternatives takes time. Alternatives are also best formulated once the analysis has progressed far enough to identify the significant impacts they are meant to address, and it may therefore be difficult to propose feasible alternatives that reduce significant effects during a preliminary process. Prop. 45 does attempt to address some challenges with the current CEQA process. For instance, the State CEQA Guidelines require evaluation of a reasonable range of alternatives but do not define what should be considered a reasonable range. Lead agencies thus sometimes require consideration of five to ten-plus alternatives, which can add time and cost to an EIR. However, while more certainty is provided by placing limits on the number of alternatives, this provision places responsibility for developing the alternative in the hands of the party with an economic interest in project approval rather than the entity, the lead agency, that is charged with reducing the significant effects of a project via mitigation or alternatives. Under the streamlined process, both the proposed alternative and the no project alternative would largely be developed before the environmental analysis has proceeded past scoping. A project’s significant impacts may not be well understood within 15 days after scoping closes. As a result, alternatives may have to be formulated before the issues they are meant to address have been fully identified.
Prop. 45 also says little about the lead agency’s discretion once the applicant submits its alternatives. Can a lead agency require substantial revisions if the proposed alternative does not meaningfully reduce significant impacts? Can it reject the applicant’s description of the no project alternative if it believes reasonably foreseeable conditions would differ materially? Beyond noting that the lead agency must certify that the applicant has met the procedural requirements of Article 5, the initiative does not address these questions.
Initial Practice Considerations for Alternatives under Proposition 45
Lead agencies may want to develop a clear set of criteria they expect in alternatives to the project, including substantial evidence to support the criteria (such as impact reduction) so that applicants have sufficient guidance to successfully achieve the alternatives certification. Lead agencies may also consider requiring an applicant to submit a preliminary assessment of potential alternatives as part of the application process.
8: TRIBAL CONSULTATION PROCESS
In Article 3, PRC Section 21016, the initiative describes an alternative process of tribal consultation for qualifying essential projects. All essential projects must follow the alternative tribal consultation process if they use the Prop. 45 streamlining provisions, per PRC Section 21015(d)(1).
The tribal consultation process pertains to consultation with “consulting tribes,” which are defined as tribes appearing on the most recent list of Federally Recognized Indian Tribes that are traditionally and culturally affiliated with the geographic area of the proposed essential project (PRC Section 21028[e][1]).
